lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: The Voice of God and The Wise Caliph
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

Unit 1.1 has two reading texts. The poem The Voice of God by Louis I. Newman tells of a man who climbed the topmost steeple (the tallest part of a religious building) to hear the voice of God, but God told him to go down again, because God dwells among the people. The story The Wise Caliph is about Caliph Haroon-ur-Rashid, who was known and respected for his justice, wisdom and concern for the welfare of his people. He used to walk through the streets of Baghdad at night in disguise to gain first-hand knowledge of the people's difficulties. One day the Qazi brought him a difficult dispute: a well-dressed rich man and a beggar in rags both claimed that a beautiful white horse belonged to them. The rich man said he had given the lame beggar a lift out of pity, but at the city gate the beggar refused to get down and claimed the horse was his. The beggar told the opposite story. The wise ruler asked each man to place his hand on the horse one by one. The horse winced at the beggar's touch, because he was a stranger, but it snorted and neighed with pleasure when the rich man touched it, because it recognised its true master. The ruler gave the horse to the rich man, and forgave the beggar on the condition that he begged the rich man's forgiveness. The rich man readily forgave him and even gave him a handful of gold coins.

The Voice of God: Key Points

  • The poet climbed the tall tower of the place of worship because he wanted to hear the voice of God.
  • He was told to come back down because God lives among the people, not only high up in a tower.
  • Message of the poem: God is found among people — by serving and caring for people, we come close to God.
  • Pre-reading: a good person is honest, kind, fair, helpful, patient and caring; a bad person is dishonest, selfish, cruel, unfair and harmful to others.
  • People who do wrong should not always be punished: small mistakes can be forgiven after an apology, but serious wrongdoing should be punished so that justice is done and others are protected.

The Wise Caliph: Key Points

  • There are four main characters: the ruler (Caliph Haroon-ur-Rashid), the Qazi, the well-dressed rich man, and the beggar in rags.
  • The Qazi brought the case to the ruler because he found it difficult and could not settle the dispute about the horse.
  • The ruler asked the beggar to touch the horse first; the horse winced because the beggar was not its master.
  • The rich man, the true owner, finally received the horse.
  • The ruler decided to be merciful: the beggar was forgiven on the condition that he asked the rich man for forgiveness.
  • The rich man forgave the beggar and gave him gold coins, so everyone liked him for being kind-hearted and generous.
  • The beggar had refused to get off the horse because he wanted to claim that the horse belonged to him; he admitted: 'Instead of thanking you for taking pity on me and giving me a lift, I lied and claimed that the horse belonged to me.'

Remember

A head of state should care for the welfare of all people, ensure justice for everyone, be honest and truthful, listen to people's problems and protect the poor and weak. He should not favour the rich over the poor, take bribes, ignore people's problems, punish anyone without proof, or use power for personal gain.

mcqs.q: In the poem 'The Voice of God', where did the man climb to hear the voice of God?
mcqs.why: The notes say the man climbed the topmost steeple, the tallest part of a religious building, hoping to hear God's voice there. The other places are not mentioned in the poem's summary at all.

options: Because the man had climbed without permission
Because God dwells among the people
Because it was time for prayer
mcqs.q: Why did God tell the man to go down again?
mcqs.why: God told him to go down because God dwells among the people, not only high up in a tower. The lesson of the poem is that God is found among people, so the man had to return to them.

options: We should climb high places to pray
God is found among people, by serving and caring for them
God speaks only inside places of worship
We should live alone, away from people
mcqs.q: What is the main message of the poem 'The Voice of God'?
mcqs.why: The notes state the message clearly: God is found among people, and by serving and caring for people we come close to God. Climbing the tower did not bring the man closer to God.

options: justice, wisdom and concern for the welfare of his people
mcqs.q: Caliph Haroon-ur-Rashid was known and respected for his:
mcqs.why: The story notes describe Haroon-ur-Rashid as known and respected for his justice, wisdom and concern for the welfare of his people. These qualities explain why he personally looked into the people's problems.

options: To gain first-hand knowledge of the people's difficulties
To find a lost white horse
mcqs.q: Why did the Caliph walk through the streets of Baghdad at night in disguise?
mcqs.why: The notes say he walked through Baghdad at night in disguise to gain first-hand knowledge of the people's difficulties. Disguised, people spoke freely, so he learned their real problems himself.

options: Two men claimed the same house
A rich man and a beggar both claimed a beautiful white horse
A beggar had stolen gold coins
Two men fought over a piece of land
mcqs.q: What was the dispute that the Qazi brought to the Caliph?
mcqs.why: The dispute was about a beautiful white horse: both the well-dressed rich man and the beggar in rags claimed it belonged to them. The Qazi found the case difficult, so he brought it to the ruler.

options: Because the beggar pulled its ear
Because the beggar was a stranger to it
Because the horse was frightened of the crowd
mcqs.q: Why did the horse wince when the beggar touched it?
mcqs.why: The horse winced at the beggar's touch because he was a stranger, not its master. This reaction was the Caliph's clever test, and it showed that the beggar's claim to the horse was false.

options: It snorted and neighed with pleasure
mcqs.q: How did the horse react when the rich man touched it?
mcqs.why: The notes say the horse snorted and neighed with pleasure when the rich man touched it, because it recognised its true master. This opposite reaction proved the rich man was the real owner.

options: That he begged the rich man's forgiveness
That he paid for the horse
That he left Baghdad at once
That he worked for the rich man
mcqs.q: On what condition did the Caliph forgive the beggar?
mcqs.why: The ruler was merciful: the beggar was forgiven on the condition that he begged the rich man's forgiveness. The beggar admitted he had lied instead of thanking the rich man for the lift.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'disguise' mean in the story?
mcqs.why: In the vocabulary list, 'disguise' means a change of appearance. The Caliph changed his appearance when he walked in Baghdad at night so that people would not recognise him as their ruler.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Express Agreement and Disagreement
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.2 Oral Communication teaches how to express agreement and disagreement politely. In Exercise 1, three friends — Amina, Hina and Mariam — discuss home medicines, and their mixed-up points have to be sorted to show who agrees and who disagrees. In Exercise 3, students prepare short dialogues on given topics, with one speaker giving an opinion, one agreeing and one disagreeing.

Useful Expressions

  • Agreement: I agree with you. Yes, that makes sense. That's right. I think we should…
  • Disagreement: I don't agree. I can't agree. I don't think so. That doesn't make sense to me, but I'll go with your idea. That's not right.
  • Amina's view: the medicines parents and grandparents give are better than doctors' medicines; most illnesses go away after a while; doctors' medicines lead to other problems.
  • Mariam's view: diseases not treated properly and on time can lead to bigger problems and more expenses; we should see a doctor if a health problem lasts more than two or three days; health is the most important thing in life.

Dialogue Topics

No.Topic for the dialogue
1All students should study up to the Masters' level.
2All of us should grow our own vegetables.
3All of us should stop eating meat.
4All people working in offices should wear uniforms.
5No animals should be allowed on the roads.

Model Dialogue

Topic: All of us should grow our own vegetables. Student 1: I believe we should all grow our own vegetables; fresh vegetables are healthy and cheap. Student 2: Yes, that makes sense. Home-grown vegetables are free from harmful sprays. Student 3: I can't agree. Many people have no land or time for gardening.

Remember

Practise the completed dialogue in three role sequences, rotating who plays Amina, Hina and Mariam, so that every student practises agreeing and disagreeing. Always give a reason with your opinion.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an expression of agreement?
mcqs.why: 'Yes, that makes sense' is listed in the notes among the useful expressions of agreement, like 'I agree with you' and 'That's right'. The other three expressions all show disagreement.

options: That doesn't make sense to me, but I'll go with your idea.
I think we should do it.
mcqs.q: Which expression shows polite disagreement but acceptance of the group's idea?
mcqs.why: The notes list 'That doesn't make sense to me, but I'll go with your idea' as a disagreement expression. It honestly says the speaker disagrees, yet politely accepts what the others have decided.

options: Doctors' medicines are always the best
Medicines should never be taken at home
The medicines parents and grandparents give are better than doctors' medicines
mcqs.q: What is Amina's view about medicines?
mcqs.why: Amina's view, as sorted in the exercise, is that the medicines parents and grandparents give are better than doctors' medicines. She also thinks most illnesses go away after a while by themselves.

options: Only when we have a high fever
If a health problem lasts more than two or three days
mcqs.q: According to Mariam, when should we see a doctor?
mcqs.why: Mariam's view is that we should see a doctor if a health problem lasts more than two or three days. She warns that diseases not treated properly and on time can lead to bigger problems.

options: Because home medicines are too expensive
Because untreated diseases can lead to bigger problems and more expenses
Because doctors visit homes for free
mcqs.q: Why does Mariam disagree with depending only on home medicines?
mcqs.why: Mariam argues that diseases not treated properly and on time can lead to bigger problems and more expenses. For her, health is the most important thing in life, so timely treatment matters.

options: All people working in offices should wear uniforms.
Students should not use mobile phones.
Every school should have a library.
mcqs.q: Which one is a dialogue topic given in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson lists five dialogue topics, and 'All people working in offices should wear uniforms' is one of them. The others, like studying to Masters level and growing our own vegetables, are also listed; the remaining choices here are not.

options: Because gardening is a good hobby only
Because vegetables in shops are always rotten
Because home-grown vegetables are free from harmful sprays
mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, why does Student 2 agree with growing our own vegetables?
mcqs.why: Student 2 agrees by saying, 'Yes, that makes sense. Home-grown vegetables are free from harmful sprays.' The agreement is supported with a reason, which is exactly what this lesson teaches.

options: Because vegetables need too much water
Because many people have no land or time for gardening
mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, why does Student 3 disagree with growing our own vegetables?
mcqs.why: Student 3 says, 'I can't agree. Many people have no land or time for gardening.' This is a clear disagreement expression followed by a practical reason, as the lesson's pattern requires.

options: Give a reason with your opinion
mcqs.q: What should you always do when you give your opinion in these dialogues?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says: always give a reason with your opinion. Both the agreeing and disagreeing students in the model dialogue support their views with reasons, and that is the skill being practised.

options: So that every student practises agreeing and disagreeing
So one student can memorise all parts
mcqs.q: Why do students rotate the roles of Amina, Hina and Mariam in practice?
mcqs.why: The notes say the completed dialogue is practised in three role sequences, rotating who plays Amina, Hina and Mariam, so that every student practises both agreeing and disagreeing, not just one side.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Capitalization and Punctuation
lessons.notes_html:
Capitalization Rules

  • Begin every sentence with a capital letter.
  • Use capital letters for proper nouns: names of people (Shah Abdul Lateef Bhitai, Sameer, Ali), places (Sindh, Quetta, Karachi, London, Nepal), rivers and buildings (the River Indus, the Faisal Mosque, the Liaquat National Hospital, Stadium Road).
  • Days, months and festivals take capitals: last July, in March.
  • Titles take capitals: Mrs Afzal, Mr Jawad; also Mount Everest.
  • The first word inside quotation marks begins with a capital letter: He said, 'My uncle's name is Asif Shaikh and he lives in London.'

Punctuation Rules

  • Use commas between items in a list: clothes, food, water, blankets and shoes.
  • Use a comma after words like Nevertheless, Moreover and However at the start of a sentence.
  • Use the exclamation mark after Hurrah!, Alas! and Wow!
  • Use a question mark at the end of every question: 'Have you finished your homework?' his mother asked.
  • Use a semicolon before 'therefore': The train began moving out of the station; therefore, the people started running.
  • Use apostrophes for contractions (don't, it's, we'll) and for possession (the girl's father, Najma's house, the gate's colour). Remember: 'its' (belonging to it) has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is'.
  • Use quotation marks for the actual words spoken, with a comma before the closing quote when the sentence continues: 'I don't know,' said Sabah.

Examples

IncorrectCorrect
the mausoleum of shah abdul lateef bhitai is in sindhThe mausoleum of Shah Abdul Lateef Bhitai is in Sindh.
sameer and ali went to quetta last julySameer and Ali went to Quetta last July.
Alas the old man is dead He suffered a lotAlas! The old man is dead. He suffered a lot.
'Have you finished your homework' his mother asked'Have you finished your homework?' his mother asked.
The girls father said, Ill take you to school today.The girl's father said, 'I'll take you to school today.'
Mother said, Wholl help me clean the house?Mother said, 'Who'll help me clean the house?'

Remember

Exercise 4 practises everything together in the ghost-house passage: Rashid tells his friends that the yellow house near the school is haunted; Sara challenges them to spend the night there to prove they do not believe in ghosts; Javed asks the others to wait for him if he is late, because he does not want to go alone.

options: sameer and ali went to quetta last july.
Sameer and Ali went to Quetta last July.
Sameer and ali went to Quetta last july.
sameer and Ali went to quetta last July.
mcqs.q: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
mcqs.why: Names of people (Sameer, Ali), places (Quetta) and months (July) are proper nouns and take capital letters, as the corrected example in the notes shows. The other options leave at least one proper noun in small letters.

options: Common nouns like house and river in general
The second word of every sentence
The first word inside quotation marks
mcqs.q: Which of these must begin with a capital letter?
mcqs.why: The rules state that the first word inside quotation marks begins with a capital letter, as in: He said, 'My uncle's name is Asif Shaikh...' Ordinary common nouns do not take capitals.

options: Both words mean exactly the same
'Its' (belonging to it) has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is'
mcqs.q: What is the difference between 'its' and 'it's'?
mcqs.why: The notes warn clearly: 'its' (belonging to it) has no apostrophe, while 'it's' with an apostrophe is the contraction of 'it is'. Mixing them up is a common punctuation mistake this lesson corrects.

mcqs.q: Which phrase shows possession with an apostrophe correctly?
mcqs.why: Apostrophes are used for possession, so 'the girl's father' is correct, like 'Najma's house' and 'the gate's colour' in the notes. The incorrect example 'The girls father' is corrected to this form.

options: To separate items in a list
mcqs.q: In the example 'The train began moving out of the station; therefore, the people started running', why is the semicolon used?
mcqs.why: The punctuation rules say to use a semicolon before 'therefore'. Here it joins two closely connected parts of one sentence instead of splitting them into two separate sentences.

mcqs.q: Which words are followed by an exclamation mark in the examples?
mcqs.why: The notes say to use the exclamation mark after Hurrah!, Alas! and Wow!, which express sudden strong feelings like joy or sorrow. For example, 'Alas! The old man is dead.' begins this way.

options: When they come at the start of a sentence
Never; commas are not used with them
mcqs.q: When is a comma used after words like 'Nevertheless', 'Moreover' and 'However'?
mcqs.why: The rules state: use a comma after words like Nevertheless, Moreover and However at the start of a sentence. Commas are also used between items in a list, such as clothes, food, water, blankets and shoes.

options: 'Have you finished your homework' his mother asked.
Have you finished your homework? his mother asked with quotes missing
'Have you finished your homework?' his mother asked.
Have you finished your homework, his mother asked!
mcqs.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
mcqs.why: A question ends with a question mark, and the actual words spoken are placed inside quotation marks: 'Have you finished your homework?' his mother asked. The first option is the incorrect version given in the exercise.

options: Titles like Mrs Afzal and Mr Jawad
The names of seasons in general
Common words like mosque and hospital alone
mcqs.q: Which of these takes a capital letter?
mcqs.why: Titles take capitals: Mrs Afzal, Mr Jawad, and also Mount Everest, as the rules state. Days, months and festivals also take capitals, as in 'last July' and 'in March'.

options: Because they come at the end of the sentence
Because they are proper nouns: a person's name and a place
Because every noun takes a capital
mcqs.q: In the corrected sentence 'The mausoleum of Shah Abdul Lateef Bhitai is in Sindh', why are these words capitalised?
mcqs.why: Shah Abdul Lateef Bhitai is the name of a person and Sindh is the name of a place; proper nouns take capital letters. The exercise corrects the all-small version to exactly this capitalised form.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

A prefix is added at the beginning of a root word and a suffix at the end. Prefixes usually change the meaning (often to the opposite), while suffixes usually change the word class, for example verb to noun or noun to adjective. Learning prefixes and suffixes helps us guess the meanings of unfamiliar words.

Words in Sentences

  • My father was feeling uneasy due to severe pain. (easy)
  • His seat on the train was very comfortable. (comfort)
  • Mr Moeen is very irregular and is often absent from his office. (regular)
  • His childish behaviour bothered everyone. (child)
  • There is a lot of pollution in our country. (pollute)
  • We must show kindness to everyone, especially the old and the weak. (kind)
  • All survived in the horrible accident, but unfortunately the driver was killed. (fortunately)
  • Rejection from the national hockey team was unbearable for me. (reject, bearable)
  • The information given by the team member was unofficial. (inform, official)

Remember

One root word can take both: happy — unhappy (prefix) — happiness (suffix); agree — disagree — agreement; use — misuse — useful; respect — disrespect — respectful.

options: At the beginning of the root word
At the end of the root word
In the middle of the root word
mcqs.q: Where is a prefix added to a word?
mcqs.why: A prefix is added at the beginning of a root word, while a suffix is added at the end. For example, 'pre' in prepay comes before 'pay', changing its meaning to 'pay in advance' in sense.

options: It joins two words into one
It deletes letters from the word
It usually changes the word class, such as verb to noun
It always makes the opposite meaning
mcqs.q: What does a suffix usually do to a word?
mcqs.why: The key points say suffixes usually change the word class, for example verb to noun or noun to adjective, as in reflect to reflection. Making the opposite meaning is what prefixes usually do instead.

mcqs.q: What is the correct word formed from 'honest' with a prefix?
mcqs.why: The prefix table gives honest to dishonest, using the prefix dis-. The other spellings are not the forms listed in the lesson, and prefixes like un- and in- do not attach to 'honest' here.

mcqs.q: 'Legal' takes the prefix il- to form:
mcqs.why: The table shows legal to illegal, and the same pattern appears in literate to illiterate and logical to illogical. The prefix il- is used before root words beginning with the letter l.

mcqs.q: Which word means 'to understand wrongly', formed from 'understand'?
mcqs.why: The lesson lists understand to misunderstand with the prefix mis-, which carries the sense of 'wrongly'. The same prefix appears in 'misuse', formed from the root word 'use'.

mcqs.q: Which suffix form is made from 'child'?
mcqs.why: The suffix table gives child to childish, and the sentence example says 'His childish behaviour bothered everyone.' The suffix -ish changes the noun 'child' into an adjective describing behaviour.

mcqs.q: 'Kind' becomes a noun meaning the quality of being kind in the word:
mcqs.why: The table gives kind to kindness, and the example sentence says 'We must show kindness to everyone.' The suffix -ness turns the adjective 'kind' into a noun naming the quality itself.

mcqs.q: Which word is formed from 'reflect' by adding a suffix?
mcqs.why: The suffix table lists reflect to reflection, where -tion changes the verb into a noun. The same -tion pattern appears in reject to rejection, pollute to pollution and attract to attraction.

mcqs.q: How does the lesson show that 'happy' can take both a prefix and a suffix?
mcqs.why: The Remember section shows one root word taking both: happy becomes unhappy with the prefix un-, and happiness with the suffix -ness. The same pattern is given for agree, use and respect.

options: Meanings of words stay the same
Only spellings of short words change
It helps us guess the meanings of unfamiliar words
It is only useful in examinations
mcqs.q: Why is learning prefixes and suffixes useful, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: The key points state that learning prefixes and suffixes helps us guess the meanings of unfamiliar words. If we know that un- often means 'not', a new word like 'unbearable' becomes easier to understand.

lessons.title: Writing: Pre-writing Strategy and Paragraph Writing
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.4 Writing teaches a pre-writing strategy — clustering (also called mind mapping). Before writing, you put the topic in the centre and join related key areas around it, then choose one key area and write a paragraph on it. The model cluster is on Sindh, with the key areas: history, climate, culture, economy and agriculture. Two more ideas that can be added are rivers (the River Indus) and festivals (such as the Urs of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai and Eid festivals).

Clusters for Practice Topics

TopicKey areas in the cluster
PollutionAir pollution, water pollution, noise pollution, causes (smoke, waste, vehicles), effects (diseases), solutions (plant trees, clean habits)
Natural DisastersFloods, earthquakes, droughts, causes, damage, safety steps, relief work
SportsCricket, hockey, football, benefits (health, teamwork, discipline), famous players, sports grounds

Model Paragraph: The Culture of Sindh

The culture of Sindh is rich and ancient. Sindh is famous for its Sufi poetry, music, and Ajrak and Sindhi topi. The shrines of saints like Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai attract visitors from far and wide. The people of Sindh love their language, poetry, and folk tales. All these things make the culture of Sindh colourful and proud.

Model Paragraph: Pollution — Causes

Pollution is caused by many human actions. Smoke from factories and vehicles pollutes the air. Waste thrown into rivers pollutes the water. Loud horns and machines create noise pollution. All these kinds of pollution harm our health and our environment. If we control smoke, manage waste, and plant more trees, we can reduce pollution.

Remember

A good paragraph has one main idea: it opens with a topic sentence, supports it with details in the middle, and ends with a closing sentence. Clustering before writing makes sure you never run out of points.

mcqs.q: Clustering, the pre-writing strategy in this lesson, is also called:
mcqs.why: Unit 1.4 teaches a pre-writing strategy called clustering, also known as mind mapping. You put the topic in the centre and join related key areas around it before you start writing.

mcqs.q: In a cluster, what is written in the centre?
mcqs.why: The method says: before writing, you put the topic in the centre and join related key areas around it. Then you choose one key area and write a paragraph on that chosen area.

options: rivers, seas, deserts and mountains only
history, climate, culture, economy and agriculture
mcqs.q: What are the key areas in the model cluster on Sindh?
mcqs.why: The model cluster on Sindh has the key areas: history, climate, culture, economy and agriculture. Two more ideas that can be added are rivers, such as the River Indus, and festivals.

options: Rivers (the River Indus) and festivals (the Urs of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai and Eid)
mcqs.q: Which two more ideas can be added to the Sindh cluster?
mcqs.why: The notes say two more ideas that can be added are rivers (the River Indus) and festivals, such as the Urs of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai and Eid festivals. These grow the cluster beyond the five first key areas.

options: It must have at least ten sentences
It opens with a topic sentence, supports it with details in the middle, and ends with a closing sentence
mcqs.q: What makes a paragraph a good paragraph, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says a good paragraph has one main idea: it opens with a topic sentence, supports it with details in the middle, and ends with a closing sentence. Both model paragraphs follow this shape.

options: Sufi poetry, music, and Ajrak and Sindhi topi
mcqs.q: The model paragraph says Sindh is famous for its:
mcqs.why: The paragraph on the culture of Sindh says Sindh is famous for its Sufi poetry, music, and Ajrak and Sindhi topi. It also mentions the shrines of saints like Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai.

mcqs.q: In the model paragraph on pollution, what pollutes the air?
mcqs.why: The paragraph states that pollution is caused by many human actions, and smoke from factories and vehicles pollutes the air. Waste thrown into rivers pollutes the water, and loud horns make noise pollution.

mcqs.q: What pollutes the water, according to the model paragraph?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says waste thrown into rivers pollutes the water. It adds that if we control smoke, manage waste and plant more trees, we can reduce pollution of all kinds.

options: It makes sure you never run out of points
It writes the closing sentence for you
mcqs.q: What is the benefit of clustering before writing?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says clustering before writing makes sure you never run out of points. By collecting key areas first, such as causes, effects and solutions for pollution, the writer always has material ready.

mcqs.q: Which items appear in the cluster for 'Natural Disasters'?
mcqs.why: The practice cluster for Natural Disasters includes floods, earthquakes and droughts, together with causes, damage, safety steps and relief work. The other practice topics are Pollution and Sports.

lessons.title: Study Skills: Collecting Points for Written and Oral Work
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.5 Study Skills teaches how to collect points for written and oral work by asking Wh-questions about a problem: Why (cause), Where (place), When (time) and How (solution). Each problem can have several possible answers, and collecting them in a table gives ready-made points for a paragraph, essay or speech.

Problems and Their Points

ProblemWhyWhereWhenHow
Water shortagePipeline broken; water tankers come lateGulberg; the whole streetSince last week; every morningEmergency call line; store water in tanks
Garbage pilesPeople throw it; dustbins are missingStreet; near the marketEvery day; after sunsetCollection system; fine those who litter
Noise pollutionFireworks; loud hornsMarriage halls; main roadsMost weekends; rush hoursBanning; keep the volume low
Unclean airSmoke; factory smokeKarachi; industrial areasAlmost whole year; in winterStrict action; plant trees
AccidentsRash driving; over-speedingOn highways; near schoolsHighway police missing; at nightProper patrolling; follow traffic rules

Key Points

lessons.title: Fun: Completing a Story
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.6 Fun completes the ghost story begun in Language Practice Exercise 4. Rashid and his friends had been challenged by Sara to spend a night in the yellow house near the school, which the newspaper called haunted. The class completes the story with the help of guiding questions: did the boys go in, who was scared, what happened inside, and what did they tell everyone afterwards?

The Completed Story

The boys decided to go in, but not all agreed — Javed was afraid. In the end, all five went in together. Inside it was dark and silent, and a sudden sound made them all jump. They stayed only a few minutes. Javed left first, and Rashid was the least scared while Sajid was the most scared. When they came out, they found no ghost at all. They told everyone that the house was only empty and dark, and there were no ghosts — fear had made the story big.

Remember

A good story ending answers the guiding questions, keeps the same characters, and closes the problem opened at the start — here, the boys learn that fear, not a ghost, made the house seem haunted.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Dignity of Work
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The central idea of the text Dignity of Work is that one should have respect for all people who work. Akhtar came home from school cross (angry), because during the social service week at school his teacher had made him dust cupboards and desks, and the headmaster's own menial work made him feel ashamed. His Uncle Inayat, who was liked by the children because he had been to many countries and told interesting stories, explained that no honest work is low. The Holy Prophet (PBUH) repaired his own shoes, mended and washed his clothes, swept his room, carried mud and building materials when the mosque was being built in Medina, and dug the trench with his companions at the Battle of Khandaq. Other great people also worked with their own hands. In developed countries people normally do their own work: the son of a high US government official delivered newspapers to be independent, and when his son was ill, the official himself delivered the newspapers so his son would not lose his customers. In China everyone, even the Prime Minister and his wife, must spend some time each year working in the fields or in a factory. Akhtar realised that all workers should be respected without discrimination, and 'Respect for all honest work' became the motto of his life.

  • The President's son took the job of whitewashing rooms in a hotel; Rukhsana read the story of the business tycoon in a newspaper.
  • Reason for the quick progress of the Chinese: everyone has to work in the field or in a factory for some time every year.
  • Successful and developed countries understand the dignity of work, and treat people who do all kinds of jobs equally.
  • We can appreciate the support staff at school by thanking them, greeting them, keeping classrooms and toilets clean, and never looking down on them.
  • Children should be engaged in chores at home and school with small, age-wise tasks, encouragement and praise — making the bed, setting the table, watering plants, a classroom cleanliness rota — not by force.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Seek and Offer Advice
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 2.2 Oral Communication teaches how to seek advice for a problem and how to offer advice politely. The seeker explains the problem clearly; the adviser listens and suggests steps, often with 'You should…' or 'If I were you, I would…'.

Useful Expressions

  • Seeking advice: What should I do? How can I make him/her understand? How can I convince them?
  • Offering advice: You should talk to him politely. If I were you, I would divide the room into two parts. I suggest he fix a daily schedule. You should also ask your teacher to guide him.

Model Dialogues

A messy sibling: A: My brother is very messy. He throws clothes and stuff all over the place, and I have to clean up every time. What should I do? B: You should talk to him politely and agree on rules. If I were you, I would divide the room into two parts and ask him to keep his part tidy. You should also ask your parents to help you set a cleaning rota.

A friend who wastes time before exams: A: My best friend does not concentrate on his studies and wastes time, and our final exams are in two weeks. How can I make him understand the importance of studying? B: You should study together and make a timetable. If I were you, I would explain gently that exams are near and that small daily steps help.

Artist or doctor: A Class X student wants to be an artist — Hala is famous for its rich artistic work — but his parents want him to become a doctor. Advice: talk to the parents calmly, show them the artwork, explain that art is also a respected profession, promise to work hard in studies too, and ask a teacher or elder to support the talk.

Problems Young People Face

ProblemAdvice
Too much screen timeLimit mobile use, fix a daily schedule, play outdoors, keep the phone away while studying
Fear of speaking EnglishPractise a little daily, speak in class, read aloud with a friend
Litter in schoolUse dustbins, hold a cleanliness drive, remind friends politely

Remember

In Exercise 2, groups of four prepare a role play with a councillor and three citizens: each citizen presents a problem, and the others offer advice in the same pattern — problem, 'What should he do?', suggestion, second opinion.

Kinds of Verbs

There are two kinds of verbs: regular and irregular. Most verbs in English are regular: their past and past participle forms both take -ed, for example wash – washed – washed, play – played – played, call – called – called. Irregular verbs do not follow this rule. The book's chart, '3 Types of some common irregular verbs', is a reference guide that helps in tense usage. mcqs.why: Most verbs in English are regular: their past and past participle forms both take -ed, for example wash – washed – washed, play – played – played. Irregular verbs do not follow this rule.

mcqs.why: The three types are: (1) all three parts the same, (2) two parts the same, and (3) all three parts different. 'Cut' keeps the same form in present, past and past participle, so it is Type 1, like cost, hit and put.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Revision of Tenses
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Present Simple Tense is used for a routine or habit, a general truth, a near future event in a timetable, and describing something or someone. Structure: base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it). Examples: I take a bath at seven in the morning. The sun rises in the east. The tournament starts next week. Their cat has blue eyes.

Present Continuous Tense is used for an action in progress, a temporary action, and a near future plan. Structure: am/is/are + verb-ing. Examples: I am writing a letter. They are having a good time. He is leaving for Chitral next week.

Present Perfect Tense is used for actions recently completed and for a past situation related to the present. Structure: has/have + past participle. Examples: She has finished her work. I have written three letters since morning.

Present Perfect Continuous Tense is used for an action continuing over a period of time up to the present. Structure: has/have + been + verb-ing, with since/for. Examples: I have been ringing the doorbell there is no answer. The water has been boiling for twenty minutes.

Examples

SentenceTense
Birds usually build their nests in the summer.Present Simple
He gets up late and dresses quickly for school.Present Simple
My friend remembers names but forgets numbers.Present Simple
Look! It is raining so hard.Present Continuous
We are learning English these days.Present Continuous
The teacher is explaining and the students are writing.Present Continuous
I have read this book twice already.Present Perfect
My brother has applied for a job.Present Perfect
Seema has completed her work as Beena has helped her throughout.Present Perfect
It has been raining for three hours continuously.Present Perfect Continuous
We have been working since twelve noon.Present Perfect Continuous
She has been cooking food for us without a break while we have been watching this match.Present Perfect Continuous

Remember

Choose Simple for habits and facts (My sister behaves nicely with everyone; His brother drinks tea three times a day), and Continuous for what is happening now or a fixed near-future plan (We are travelling to Gilgit tomorrow; Our uncle is coming to our house this weekend). 'Usually' with 'but today' shows the contrast: My mother usually watches television at this time but today she is sleeping.

mcqs.q: The Present Simple Tense is used for:
mcqs.why: The rules say Present Simple is used for a routine or habit, a general truth, a near future event in a timetable, and describing something. Its structure is the base verb, with s/es added for he, she or it.

mcqs.q: Which example shows Present Simple used for a timetable event?
mcqs.why: 'The tournament starts next week' is given as Present Simple for a near future event in a timetable. Although it speaks of the future, a fixed timetable takes the Present Simple form.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of the Present Continuous Tense?
mcqs.why: Present Continuous is formed with am/is/are + verb-ing, as in 'I am writing a letter.' It is used for an action in progress, a temporary action, and a near future plan.

mcqs.q: 'He is leaving for Chitral next week' is an example of:
mcqs.why: The notes list 'He is leaving for Chitral next week' under Present Continuous, because that tense is also used for a near future plan. The action is not happening now, but the plan is fixed.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of the Present Perfect Tense?
mcqs.why: Present Perfect is formed with has/have + past participle, as in 'She has finished her work.' It is used for actions recently completed and for a past situation related to the present.

mcqs.q: 'I have read this book twice already' is:
mcqs.why: The examples table marks 'I have read this book twice already' as Present Perfect. The form have + past participle (read) shows a completed action connected with the present.

mcqs.q: 'It has been raining for three hours continuously' is:
mcqs.why: This sentence is listed as Present Perfect Continuous: has/have + been + verb-ing, used with since/for for an action continuing over a period of time up to the present.

options: Since morning, in 'I have written three letters since morning'
All of these can be used with time periods in these tenses
mcqs.q: Which time expression appears with the Perfect tenses in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The examples use since and for with the perfect forms: 'written three letters since morning', 'boiling for twenty minutes' and 'working since twelve noon'. Since marks a starting point and for marks a length of time.

mcqs.q: 'Look! It is raining so hard' is an example of:
mcqs.why: The table marks this Present Continuous, and the word 'Look!' points to an action in progress at this moment. The structure is 'is raining', is + verb-ing, matching the rule.

options: Present Simple for the habit and Present Continuous for today

mcqs.why: The Remember section explains this contrast: 'usually' with 'but today' — Present Simple (watches) for the habit, and Present Continuous (is sleeping) for what is happening now instead.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Simple and Compound Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

A simple sentence has one independent clause — one subject and one verb — and expresses one complete idea. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction. The seven coordinating conjunctions are remembered as FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. A comma usually comes before the conjunction in a compound sentence. (In the book's numbering for 2.3, this set is Exercises 10–12; there is no Exercise 8 or 9 in this section.)

Examples

SentenceType
You have been sleeping since morning.Simple
I don't know the answer.Simple
He is totally dependent on his parents.Simple
No one is traveling these days.Simple
I want to lose weight, yet I eat chocolates daily.Compound
Atif is famous, but he is very humble.Compound
You may eat a mango or have mango pickle.Compound
He was feeling sick, so he went to the doctor.Compound
I go to the library, for I love reading.Compound
He is rich and he has a good heart.Compound

Key Points

  • A compound sentence can be split into two simple sentences: 'Atif is famous, but he is very humble' becomes 'Atif is famous. He is very humble.'
  • 'He was feeling sick, so he went to the doctor' becomes 'He was feeling sick. He went to the doctor.'
  • 'I go to the library, for I love reading' becomes 'I go to the library. I love reading.'

Remember

Count the clauses: one clause = simple sentence; two clauses joined by a FANBOYS word = compound sentence.

options: One independent clause — one subject and one verb
One subject with three verbs only
mcqs.q: A simple sentence has:
mcqs.why: A simple sentence has one independent clause — one subject and one verb — and expresses one complete idea. For example, 'I don't know the answer' is a simple sentence in the lesson's table.

mcqs.why: The table marks this sentence Compound: two independent clauses are joined by the FANBOYS word 'yet', and a comma usually comes before the conjunction in a compound sentence.

mcqs.why: The key points show that a compound sentence can be split into two simple sentences, and this one becomes 'He was feeling sick. He went to the doctor.' The conjunction 'so' is removed when splitting.

mcqs.why: The conjunction is 'for', one of the FANBOYS words, giving the reason for going to the library. Split, the sentence becomes 'I go to the library. I love reading.'

options: Usually, before the conjunction in a compound sentence

mcqs.why: The rules state that a comma usually comes before the conjunction in a compound sentence, as in 'You may eat a mango or have mango pickle' pattern examples like 'Atif is famous, but he is very humble.'

Subject: Request for Information about Admission, Uniform, and Attendance Policy. Dear Sir/Madam, I am a student of Class X, and I wish to seek admission to your college after my board examinations. lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: King Bruce and the Spider
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The poem King Bruce and the Spider, written by Eliza Cook, tells how a sad king learnt never to give up. King Bruce of Scotland was unhappy, sad and in despair, because he had tried and tried to do a great deed to make his people glad, but he could not succeed, and he decided to give it all up. Just then, a spider dropping down on its silken thread attracted his attention, and he stopped his thinking to watch what it would do. The spider was trying to climb to its cobweb home, a long way up at the ceiling dome, hanging by a very fine thread. Again and again it climbed, slipped and fell — nine brave attempts were counted. After one fall it lay a little dizzy and faint, but when its head grew steady, it went up again without complaint. The king thought it would now give up, but the spider kept trying, at different speeds, sometimes fast and sometimes slow, and near its home it moved steadily, steadily, inch by inch, higher and higher. A bold little run at the very last put it into its home. The king cried, 'All honour to those who try,' braced his mind, and tried once more as he had tried before — and that time he did not fail.

Key Points

  • King Bruce cared for his people: he had tried and tried to do a great deed to make them glad.
  • Before he saw the spider, he had decided to give up everything in hopelessness.
  • He thought the spider would not reach its home because the way was long, the thread very fine, and he could not work out how it would get there.
  • The spider made nine brave attempts that were counted, and succeeded on the next try — it did not make more than twenty attempts.
  • When it slipped down it did not stay on the ground; each time it climbed up again.
  • The lesson the king learnt: those who try again and again succeed; like the spider, he too could succeed if he did not give up.
  • Moral of the poem: try, try again — those who keep trying, succeed.
  • A spider can teach us something: it keeps trying again and again until it reaches its web; most spiders cannot hurt us.

Vocabulary

Remember

In Exercise 7, groups prepare a brief role-play on any story with a moral. Model — The Hare and the Tortoise: the proud hare runs far ahead and sleeps under a tree; the tortoise keeps walking slowly and steadily and reaches the finish line first. Moral: slow and steady wins the race; never be proud and careless.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Revision of Past Tense
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Past Simple Tense shows an action completed in the past. Structure: second form of the verb. Example: We ate delicious food at their house. The guard closed and locked the gate before going to bed.

Past Continuous Tense shows an action in progress at a past time, often with 'while' for two actions going on together. Structure: was/were + verb-ing. Example: My sister was doing her homework while I was washing dishes.

Past Perfect Tense shows the earlier of two past actions. Structure: had + past participle. Example: She had died before they reached the hospital.

Past Perfect Continuous Tense shows an action that continued up to a point in the past. Structure: had been + verb-ing, usually with for/since. Example: He had been crying for help for five hours when the rescue team finally arrived.

Examples

SentenceTense
The mouse ran under the cupboard.Past Simple
The house in which we lived till last year belonged to my uncle.Past Simple
The parrots made a lot of noise so we sold them.Past Simple
The papers were flying in all directions due to strong winds.Past Continuous
The boys were fighting over who would play first.Past Continuous
We were shaking the tree and the ripe fruits were falling on the ground.Past Continuous
We had spent a lot of money on buying gifts, so we decided to stop.Past Perfect
The students had finished their work and had left for home when the rain started.Past Perfect
I had been reading for two hours before I fell asleep.Past Perfect Continuous
The bell had been ringing and the dog had been barking for nearly 20 minutes before someone opened the door.Past Perfect Continuous
The MET department had been warning about a storm but the people had been refusing to listen.Past Perfect Continuous

Story Practice: Kakenya Ntaiya

Exercise 3 fills the story of Kakenya Ntaiya of Kenya with Past Simple and Past Continuous forms: when she was fourteen, she requested her father to let her finish high school; very few Maasai girls ever finished high school, but her father accepted; she won a scholarship to the USA; the villagers all came to see her off, and Ntaiya was crying as she was leaving. Later she worked at the UN, got a doctorate, returned home and set up a primary school in her village, which provided education to more than 150 girls.

Remember

For two past actions, the earlier one takes the Past Perfect and the later one the Past Simple: 'As soon as Samina had swept the yard there was a storm.' For an action continuing up to a past moment, use had been + verb-ing with for/since.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of the Past Simple Tense?
mcqs.why: Past Simple shows an action completed in the past, and its structure is the second form of the verb, as in 'We ate delicious food at their house.' 'Ate' is the second form of eat.

mcqs.q: 'My sister was doing her homework while I was washing dishes' is:
mcqs.why: This example is given for Past Continuous: was/were + verb-ing, showing an action in progress at a past time. The word 'while' joins two actions that were going on together.

options: It shows the earlier of two past actions
It shows an action happening now
mcqs.q: What does the Past Perfect Tense show?
mcqs.why: Past Perfect shows the earlier of two past actions, with the structure had + past participle: 'She had died before they reached the hospital.' The dying happened before the reaching.

mcqs.q: 'He had been crying for help for five hours when the rescue team finally arrived' is:
mcqs.why: The example illustrates Past Perfect Continuous: had been + verb-ing, usually with for/since, showing an action that continued up to a point in the past — the arrival of the rescue team.

mcqs.q: 'The mouse ran under the cupboard' is:
mcqs.why: The examples table marks this Past Simple: 'ran' is the second form of run, showing a single action completed in the past, with no was/were or had structure in the sentence.

mcqs.q: 'We had spent a lot of money on buying gifts, so we decided to stop' — the first verb phrase is:
mcqs.why: 'Had spent' is had + past participle, so it is Past Perfect, showing the earlier action. The later action, 'decided', is in Past Simple, exactly as the Remember rule describes.

mcqs.q: 'I had been reading for two hours before I fell asleep' is:
mcqs.why: This is listed as Past Perfect Continuous: had been + verb-ing with 'for two hours', showing reading continued up to the past moment when the speaker fell asleep.

options: Only Past Simple in both actions
The earlier action takes Past Perfect and the later one Past Simple
The earlier action takes Past Simple and the later one Past Perfect
mcqs.q: For two past actions, what is the rule given in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The Remember section states: for two past actions, the earlier one takes the Past Perfect and the later one the Past Simple — 'As soon as Samina had swept the yard there was a storm.'

options: She requested her father to let her finish high school
She won a prize in a race
mcqs.q: In the story practice, what did Kakenya Ntaiya do when she was fourteen?
mcqs.why: Exercise 3 tells that when Ntaiya was fourteen, she requested her father to let her finish high school. Very few Maasai girls ever finished high school, but her father accepted her request.

mcqs.why: The story says she returned home and set up a primary school in her village, which provided education to more than 150 girls. Earlier she had won a scholarship to the USA and worked at the UN.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Revision of Articles
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

A / An (indefinite articles) are used before a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time or in general. Use an before a vowel sound: an honest man (h is silent), an honour, an example, an old friend, an Australian sheep. Use a before a consonant sound: a giraffe, a crook, a cup of tea, a factory, a uniform ('u' sounds like 'yu'), a hotel. No article is used before plural nouns in general or uncountable nouns: boil eggs, make sandwiches, good wool.

The (definite article) is used before a particular person or thing, before superlatives (the most spoken language, the persons I love the most), before unique or well-known things (the English language, the telephone's inventor), and with certain names (the USA, the UAE, the River Indus, the Khyber Pass, the central library). No article is used before proper names of people (Graham Bell), before countries like Pakistan, Afghanistan, before languages, history, trade and goods in a general sense, and before general plural nouns (lions are dangerous animals).

Examples

SentencePoint shown
A giraffe has a long neck.a + consonant sound
He is an honest man but his friend is a crook.an before silent h
It was an honour to be nominated.an before silent h
An old friend is staying at a hotel on the River Indus.an/a first mention; the + river name
The English language is the most spoken language in the world.the + language; the + superlative
My sister lives in the USA.the + country name with states
When you drive a car in the UAE, you must keep to the right.the + UAE; the right (direction)
The inventor of the telephone was Graham Bell.the + particular person; no article before a name
There are beautiful flowers in the park.no article before a general plural
The butcher opposite the library sells good meat.the + particular shop/library; no article before uncountable 'meat'

Paragraph Practice: The Khyber Pass

Exercise 9 completes the Khyber Pass paragraph: 'Who has not heard of the famous Khyber Pass in Pakistan? It is a narrow mountain valley in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. We can go to the Khyber Pass from Peshawar. Many people who want to go to Afghanistan cross the border from the Khyber Pass. The Khyber Pass has been famous in history for thousands of years. The Aryans crossed it to reach the sub-continent about four thousand years ago. After them came the Mongols and the Tartars. Moreover, the Khyber Pass is an ancient trade route used by the caravans carrying bales of cotton and silk.'

Remember

Choose a/an by SOUND, not by letter: a uniform, an hour. Use 'the' when the listener knows exactly which one; leave the article out for things spoken of in general.

options: Before a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time or in general
Only before words starting with a vowel letter
mcqs.q: When are 'a' and 'an' used?
mcqs.why: A/An, the indefinite articles, are used before a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time or in general. No article is used before plural nouns in general or uncountable nouns, like 'good wool'.

options: Because 'honest' starts with the letter h
Because it is a long word
Because the 'h' in 'honest' is silent, so it begins with a vowel sound
mcqs.q: Why do we say 'an honest man' and not 'a honest man'?
mcqs.why: The rule is to choose a/an by sound, not by letter: 'an' is used before a vowel sound, and in 'honest' the h is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound. The same applies to 'an honour' and 'an hour'.

mcqs.q: Which is correct: ___ uniform?
mcqs.why: The notes give 'a uniform' because here 'u' sounds like 'yu', a consonant sound, so 'a' is used. This is the classic proof that we choose a/an by sound, not by the written letter.

options: Before plural nouns like lions in general
Before languages like English in general
Before superlatives, such as 'the most spoken language'
mcqs.q: When is 'the' used in the examples?
mcqs.why: 'The' is used before superlatives: 'the most spoken language' and 'the persons I love the most'. It is also used before a particular person or thing and before unique or well-known things.

mcqs.q: Which is correct for the country name in 'My sister lives in ___'?
mcqs.why: The example sentence is 'My sister lives in the USA.' Names like the USA and the UAE take 'the', while countries like Pakistan and Afghanistan take no article before them.

options: No article: 'The inventor of the telephone was Graham Bell'
mcqs.q: How is the name Graham Bell used in the example?
mcqs.why: No article is used before proper names of people, so the sentence is 'The inventor of the telephone was Graham Bell.' Here 'the' is used for the particular person, the inventor, but not before his name.

options: The park has the before it because the flowers are general
Beautiful flowers in general take no article, as in 'There are beautiful flowers in the park'
mcqs.q: Why is there no article before 'flowers' in the park example?
mcqs.why: The table notes: no article before a general plural — 'There are beautiful flowers in the park.' Compare 'lions are dangerous animals', where the general plural also takes no article.

options: No article is used before the uncountable noun 'meat' used in a general sense
mcqs.q: In 'The butcher opposite the library sells good meat', why does 'meat' have no article?
mcqs.why: The table explains: the + particular shop/library, but no article before the uncountable 'meat'. Uncountable nouns spoken of in general, like wool and meat, are used without an article.

options: A narrow mountain valley in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, reached from Peshawar
mcqs.q: What is the Khyber Pass, as the paragraph describes it?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says the Khyber Pass is a narrow mountain valley in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, and we can go to it from Peshawar. People cross the border to Afghanistan from the Khyber Pass.

options: The Aryans crossed it to reach the sub-continent about four thousand years ago
mcqs.q: Who crossed the Khyber Pass in ancient times, according to the paragraph?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says the Aryans crossed it to reach the sub-continent about four thousand years ago, and after them came the Mongols and the Tartars. It is also an ancient trade route for caravans carrying cotton and silk.

lessons.title: Writing: Summary of a Poem
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 3.4 Writing teaches how to write a summary of a poem: name the poem and the poet, then go stanza by stanza, saying what the poet says in each, and finish with one line beginning 'In all, the poem teaches us…'.

Model Summary: Little Things by Julia Carney

The poem 'Little Things' is a simple children's song by Julia Carney. It explains that even little things are important. In the first stanza, the poet says that little drops of water and little grains of sand make the mighty ocean and the pleasant land. In the second stanza, she says that little deeds of kindness and little words of love make our world an Eden like the heaven above. In all, the poem teaches us that small things, done with kindness and love, build great results.

Model Summary: The Man Who Wins (Anonymous)

The poem 'The Man Who Wins' is by an anonymous poet. It explains that success begins in the mind. In the first stanza, the poet says if you think you are beaten, you are; if you think you cannot win, you almost certainly will not. In the second stanza, he says success begins with a fellow's will — it is all in the state of mind. In the third stanza, he says you must think high to rise and be sure of yourself before you can win a prize. In the last stanza, he says life's battles do not always go to the stronger or faster man; sooner or later the man who wins is the man who thinks he can. In all, the poem teaches that self-belief and a positive mind bring success.

Remember

A poem summary keeps the order of the stanzas, uses your own words, and ends with the poem's overall teaching.

options: Copy the poem line by line
Name the poem and the poet, go stanza by stanza, and finish with one line beginning 'In all, the poem teaches us…'
Count the lines of the poem
mcqs.q: How should a summary of a poem be written?
mcqs.why: Unit 3.4 teaches: name the poem and the poet, then go stanza by stanza saying what the poet says in each, and finish with one line beginning 'In all, the poem teaches us…'. Both model summaries follow this method.

options: Julia Carney wrote 'The Man Who Wins'
mcqs.q: Who wrote 'Little Things'?
mcqs.why: The model summary says 'Little Things' is a simple children's song by Julia Carney. The other model poem, 'The Man Who Wins', is by an anonymous poet, so the two must not be confused.

mcqs.q: What does the first stanza of 'Little Things' say?
mcqs.why: In the first stanza, the poet says that little drops of water and little grains of sand make the mighty ocean and the pleasant land. Small things together build great results, which is the poem's idea.

options: Little deeds of kindness and little words of love make our world an Eden like the heaven above
They are less important than big deeds
mcqs.q: What does the second stanza of 'Little Things' say?
mcqs.why: In the second stanza, she says that little deeds of kindness and little words of love make our world an Eden like the heaven above. So small kind acts, not only big ones, shape our world.

mcqs.q: Which poem teaches that success begins in the mind?
mcqs.why: The model summary of 'The Man Who Wins' (Anonymous) explains that success begins in the mind. Its first stanza says: if you think you are beaten, you are; if you think you cannot win, you almost certainly will not.

options: Success begins with a fellow's will — it is all in the state of mind
Success comes only from rich parents
mcqs.q: What does the second stanza of 'The Man Who Wins' say?
mcqs.why: The summary states that in the second stanza the poet says success begins with a fellow's will — it is all in the state of mind. This is why the poem's teaching is about self-belief.

options: The strongest man always wins first
Battles go only to the fastest man
Life's battles do not always go to the stronger or faster man; the man who wins is the man who thinks he can
mcqs.q: What does the last stanza of 'The Man Who Wins' say?
mcqs.why: In the last stanza, the poet says life's battles do not always go to the stronger or faster man; sooner or later the man who wins is the man who thinks he can. Positive thinking is the poem's final point.

options: It ends with the poem's overall teaching
mcqs.q: What does a poem summary do at the end?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says a poem summary keeps the order of the stanzas, uses your own words, and ends with the poem's overall teaching — the 'In all, the poem teaches us…' line.

options: Adding your own examples from life
mcqs.q: What language should a poem summary use?
mcqs.why: A good summary uses your own words rather than copying the poem. The model summaries retell each stanza in simple prose while keeping the poem's order and meaning.

options: You must think high to rise and be sure of yourself before you can win a prize
You must be taller than others
You must win every prize in school
You must rise early in the morning
mcqs.q: What does the third stanza of 'The Man Who Wins' say?
mcqs.why: The summary states that in the third stanza the poet says you must think high to rise and be sure of yourself before you can win a prize. Confidence must come before victory, in the poet's view.

lessons.title: Study Skills: Free Writing
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 3.5 Study Skills teaches free writing: write continuously on a topic for a fixed time — five minutes in Exercise 1, seven minutes in Exercise 2 — without stopping to correct mistakes. Free writing helps you get ideas onto paper quickly and removes the fear of the blank page.

Model Free Writing: What Do I Want to Do after I Complete My Matric?

After I complete my matric, I want to study science in college. I want to work hard and get good marks. I think about becoming a doctor because I want to help sick people. My parents want me to study well. I also want to learn computer skills. I feel happy when I think about my future. I will try my best and never give up. I know the road is long, but I will keep going step by step.

Model Free Writing: Sports

I love sports. I play cricket with my friends in the evening. Cricket keeps me fit and happy. I also like football. Sports teach us teamwork and discipline. When we play, we learn to win and to lose. I watch cricket matches on television. My favourite player works hard and never gives up. Sports keep our bodies strong and our minds fresh. I want to play every day and stay healthy.

Remember

In free writing, keep the pen moving for the full time. Do not stop for spelling or grammar — ideas first, correction later.

options: Writing continuously on a topic for a fixed time without stopping to correct mistakes
mcqs.q: What is free writing?
mcqs.why: Free writing means writing continuously on a topic for a fixed time — five minutes in Exercise 1 and seven minutes in Exercise 2 — without stopping to correct mistakes. It removes the fear of the blank page.

options: Write only when sure of spelling
mcqs.q: What is the golden rule of free writing?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says: in free writing, keep the pen moving for the full time; do not stop for spelling or grammar — ideas first, correction later. Stopping to correct breaks the flow of ideas.

options: Five minutes in Exercise 1 and seven minutes in Exercise 2
mcqs.q: How long do the free writing exercises last?
mcqs.why: The lesson fixes the time: five minutes in Exercise 1 and seven minutes in Exercise 2. Writing against a fixed short time is what pushes ideas onto paper quickly.

options: It helps you get ideas onto paper quickly and removes the fear of the blank page
mcqs.q: How does free writing help a student?
mcqs.why: The About section says free writing helps you get ideas onto paper quickly and removes the fear of the blank page. Many students fear starting; continuous writing breaks that fear.

He wants to study science in college and become a doctor to help sick people

mcqs.why: The model says: 'After I complete my matric, I want to study science in college… I think about becoming a doctor because I want to help sick people.' He also wants to learn computer skills.

'I will stop if I fail once'
mcqs.q: Which line from the model free writing shows determination?
mcqs.why: The model writer says, 'I will try my best and never give up. I know the road is long, but I will keep going step by step.' This determination is part of the model's positive ending.

options: Cricket with his friends in the evening, and he also likes football
mcqs.q: In the 'Sports' model, what does the writer play?
mcqs.why: The Sports model says: 'I play cricket with my friends in the evening. Cricket keeps me fit and happy. I also like football.' He also watches cricket matches on television.

mcqs.q: What do sports teach us, according to the model?
mcqs.why: The model says sports teach us teamwork and discipline, and when we play, we learn to win and to lose. Sports also keep our bodies strong and our minds fresh.

options: Keep the pen moving for the full time
mcqs.q: During free writing, if you make a spelling mistake, what should you do?
mcqs.why: The rule is to keep the pen moving for the full time and not stop for spelling or grammar. Correction comes later, after the fixed time ends and the ideas are safely on paper.

His favourite player is the richest
His favourite player plays only in finals

mcqs.why: The model says: 'My favourite player works hard and never gives up.' This is given as a quality the writer admires, matching the model's theme of effort in sports.

mcqs.why: The Remember section teaches the whole family together: make a promise, keep a promise, break a promise. Learning the whole phrase together, not word by word, is the lesson's main advice.

lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The text Social Media explains that social media means interactive websites and applications that enable users to create and share information, videos, thoughts and ideas, and to communicate with others. Since the advent of the internet, social media has revolutionized the concept of communication and community: one has become a part of the global community, and the speed with which social media users are rising is stupendous. It is used by people of all ages — students, professionals, businesspersons, employers and family members. The writer's conclusion is that social media is neither wholly good nor wholly bad: it has both pros and cons, numerous advantages and its share of disadvantages, and it should be used with care. A prudent user can benefit a lot from it, while a careless user can become a victim of its adverse effects. The ills of social media can be mitigated if we follow certain basic rules, and giving it up altogether may not be a realistic option in today's times.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Individual Presentation
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 4.2 Oral Communication teaches the presentation skills framework for an individual presentation. A good presentation follows a clear pattern: greet the audience and introduce yourself, name your topic, say how long you will take, divide the topic into parts with signpost words (First, Secondly, Lastly), give an example, and end with a conclusion and thanks.

Presentation Framework

  • Opening: Good morning, everyone. My name is Ahmed, your class fellow.
  • Topic: Today, I would like to say a few words about keeping our surroundings clean.
  • Time: I will probably take about five minutes.
  • Structure: I have divided my topic into three parts. First… Secondly… Lastly…
  • Example: For example, our class cleans the school garden every Friday.
  • Conclusion: In conclusion, cleanliness is everyone's duty. Thank you for your time.
  • Other useful openers: 'I am here to talk about…', 'I am going to give you an overview of…', 'I hope to be finished in five minutes', 'This should last only a few minutes', 'To sum up…', 'Therefore, every drop counts.'

Presentation Topics and Their Points

TopicMain points
Keeping our surroundings cleanCleanliness keeps us healthy and happy; throw rubbish in dustbins, clean classrooms, plant trees; cleanliness is everyone's duty
Making Pakistan greenTrees give clean air and rain and stop floods; plant trees in schools, homes and streets and look after them; do not cut trees or waste water
Overcoming water shortage problemsCauses: wasting water, growing population, little rain, leaking taps; solutions: save water, repair leaks, store rainwater

Why we should plant trees (own choice)Trees give clean air, shade, fruits and rain; people are cutting trees; each of us should plant at least one tree and look after it

Remember

Every model presentation in this lesson follows the same framework, so learn the framework once and use it for any topic: greeting, name, topic, time, three parts, example, conclusion, thanks.

Ask questions to the audience first
