lessons.title: Oral Communication: Polite Forms to Negotiate and Develop Consensus
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 7.2 Oral Communication teaches polite forms used to negotiate and to develop consensus (agreement by all). In Exercise 1, students practise the book's dialogue between a client and a travel agent — the client complains that the trip was a disaster, a high price was charged and low services were provided; the agent apologises and offers to return half of the price paid, and the client accepts: 'This sounds great to me. Thank you.' Roles are then reversed and practised again.

Negotiating Phrases

  • Giving an opinion: In my opinion, we should spend most on the dress. Let's see, we have 5,000 rupees.
  • A different idea: I have a different idea. I think we should spend 2,500 on the dress, 1,500 on the bag, and 1,000 on the footwear.
  • Opening discussion: Let's discuss this.
  • Agreeing with a suggestion: This sounds good. I agree with you. I like this idea.
  • Closing the matter: We can sort this out.

Model Consensus: The Class Outing

Student 1: In my opinion, we should go to the beach because it is near and everyone can enjoy it. Student 2: I have a different idea. I think we should go to Makli because it is a historical place. Student 3: Let's discuss this. The beach is enjoyable, but Makli is far. Student 4: Let's see, Ranikot and Hub dam are also far. Student 1: We can sort this out: let us go to the beach this time, and visit Makli next time. Student 2: This sounds good. Student 3: I agree with you. Student 4: I like this idea. All: We agree to go to the beach.

Remember

Consensus is not voting against anyone: hear every idea, discuss distances, cost and benefit, then adjust the plan — 'beach this time, Makli next time' — until everyone can honestly say 'I agree'.

mcqs.why: The agent apologises and offers to return half of the price paid, and the client accepts: 'This sounds great to me. Thank you.' This polite offer is the negotiation's turning point.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Revision of Prepositions (Movement and Direction)
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Prepositions of movement and direction show where something or someone is going: to (destination), into (entering), onto (moving to a surface), across (from one side to the other), through (inside and out the other side), around (in a circle / in the area), over (above and across), under (below, passing beneath), past (beyond a point), towards (in the direction of), from (starting point), by (alongside), up / down (along a slope). Note the difference between 'in'/'on' (position) and 'into'/'onto' (movement).

Examples

SentencePoint shown
Let's go for a walk by the river.by = alongside
I'm going to the shop to buy some grocery.to = destination
We sailed around the bay today.around
Let's walk through the forest.through
We walked all around the city centre but couldn't find the store.around
The lion walked in a circle around the baby giraffe before attacking it.around
The train passed through nine tunnels on the way to Peshawar.through
His dog is always trying to escape from the backyard.from
Be careful when you walk across the street.across
A flock of birds is flying over the trees under the blue sky.over
She walked into the kitchen and put her packages on the table.into (movement) / on (position)
River Kunhar flows towards the lake.towards
The door was locked, so I shoved the letter under the door.under
I slipped as I stepped onto the platform.onto

Remember

Ask 'where to?' to test a movement preposition: across the street (side to side), through the tunnel (in one end, out the other), around the station (a circle or an area walk), over our houses (above), under the door (beneath).

options: to, into, onto, across, through, around, over, under, past, towards, from, by, up and down
mcqs.q: Which set lists prepositions of movement and direction?
mcqs.why: Prepositions of movement and direction show where something or someone is going: to, into, onto, across, through, around, over, under, past, towards, from, by, up/down. 'In' and 'on' show position instead.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between 'into/onto' and 'in/on'?
mcqs.why: The rules note the difference between 'in'/'on' (position) and 'into'/'onto' (movement). Example: 'She walked into the kitchen (movement) and put her packages on the table (position).'

mcqs.why: The example table says: 'Let's go for a walk by the river' — by = alongside. By contrast, 'to' shows destination, as in 'I'm going to the shop to buy some grocery.'

mcqs.why: The example is: 'The train passed through nine tunnels on the way to Peshawar.' Through means inside and out the other side — in one end of the tunnel and out the other.

options: across, in 'Be careful when you walk across the street'
mcqs.q: Which preposition means 'from one side to the other'?
mcqs.why: Across means from one side to the other: 'Be careful when you walk across the street.' The Remember section repeats the test: across the street (side to side), through the tunnel (in one end, out the other).

options: The dog escaped into the backyard
The dog escaped onto the backyard
The dog escaped across the backyard
His dog is always trying to escape from the backyard — 'from' shows the starting point
mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'from' for a starting point?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'His dog is always trying to escape from the backyard.' From marks the starting point of the movement, just as 'to' marks the destination.

options: over, in 'A flock of birds is flying over the trees'
mcqs.q: Which preposition shows 'above and across'?
mcqs.why: Over means above and across: 'A flock of birds is flying over the trees under the blue sky.' Under is its opposite — below, passing beneath, as in the letter shoved under the door.

options: towards, in 'River Kunhar flows towards the lake'
mcqs.q: Which preposition shows direction without arrival?
mcqs.why: Towards means in the direction of: 'River Kunhar flows towards the lake.' It points the way the movement goes, unlike 'to', which names the destination reached.

options: stepped onto the platform, in 'I slipped as I stepped onto the platform'
mcqs.q: Which uses 'onto' for moving to a surface?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'I slipped as I stepped onto the platform.' Onto shows movement to a surface, while 'on' alone would only show position on that surface.

options: Ask 'where to?' to test a movement preposition
mcqs.q: How can you test a movement preposition?
mcqs.why: The Remember section advises: ask 'where to?' to test a movement preposition — across the street (side to side), through the tunnel (in one end, out the other), around the station (a circle or an area walk), over our houses (above), under the door (beneath).

lessons.title: Language Practice: Compound Prepositions
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

A compound preposition is a preposition made of two or more words that works as one unit, for example: on account of, in addition to, away from, according to, because of, next to, in return for, as to, in front of, in case of, in spite of, due to. Use the whole phrase as it is; do not break it or change its words.

Examples

SentenceCompound preposition
He can't perform any more on account of his failing health.on account of
The villagers had to carry pails of water in addition to their work in the fields.in addition to
Sameer was never away from his parents going to the city.away from
This theory is wrong according to his philosophy.according to
The match was delayed because of rain.because of
This dog has been sitting next to me for one hour.next to
I gave him a new book in return for the one I lost.in return for
We will inform you later, as to the situation.as to
The van stopped in front of the hospital.in front of
You will have to leave your position in case of any change in the plan.in case of

Passage Practice

Exercise 4 completes a travel passage with prepositions used once each: 'One hot summer morning, in spite of the intense heat, we decided to take a trip out of the city and go to the ocean. We got into the car and drove on the highway, which went up one side of the mountain and came down the other side. Then the highway went around a part of the lake and over the bridge. After that we drove through the forest and past the big water tower. We arrived at the beach by noon due to the heavy traffic. According to the map, the water that flowed in the river came from the melted glaciers. Natives preferred to live on top of the mountain as they felt safe there.'

Remember

Learn compound prepositions as fixed phrases: because of / due to / on account of (reason); in spite of (contrast); in front of / next to (place); in addition to (adding); in case of (condition).

options: A preposition made of two or more words that works as one unit
A preposition with a capital letter
Two separate prepositions in one sentence
mcqs.q: What is a compound preposition?
mcqs.why: A compound preposition is a preposition made of two or more words that works as one unit, for example on account of, in addition to, according to and in spite of. The whole phrase must be used as it is.

options: on account of, in 'He can't perform any more on account of his failing health'
mcqs.q: Which example uses 'on account of'?
mcqs.why: The example table gives: 'He can't perform any more on account of his failing health — on account of.' On account of belongs to the reason group with because of and due to.

options: The villagers had to carry pails of water in addition to their work in the fields
The dog sat next to me
The van stopped in front of the hospital
mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'in addition to'?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'The villagers had to carry pails of water in addition to their work in the fields.' In addition to is the adding compound preposition in the Remember groups.

options: because of, in 'The match was delayed because of rain'
mcqs.q: Which compound preposition shows a reason in the match example?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'The match was delayed because of rain — because of.' Reason compound prepositions are because of, due to and on account of.

options: next to, in 'This dog has been sitting next to me for one hour'
mcqs.q: Which compound preposition shows place beside someone?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'This dog has been sitting next to me for one hour — next to.' Place compound prepositions in the lesson are in front of and next to.

options: in return for, in 'I gave him a new book in return for the one I lost'
mcqs.q: Which phrase means 'in exchange'?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'I gave him a new book in return for the one I lost — in return for.' It shows something given back in exchange for something else.

options: in front of the hospital, in 'The van stopped in front of the hospital'
mcqs.q: The van stopped where, in the example?
mcqs.why: The example sentence is: 'The van stopped in front of the hospital — in front of.' In front of is a place compound preposition, like next to.

options: in case of, in 'You will have to leave your position in case of any change in the plan'
mcqs.q: Which phrase shows a condition?
mcqs.why: The example is: 'You will have to leave your position in case of any change in the plan — in case of.' The Remember section groups in case of under condition.

options: in spite of, in 'One hot summer morning, in spite of the intense heat, we decided to take a trip'
mcqs.q: In the travel passage, which phrase shows contrast?
mcqs.why: The passage begins: 'One hot summer morning, in spite of the intense heat, we decided to take a trip out of the city.' In spite of is the contrast compound preposition in the Remember groups.

options: Use only the first word of the phrase
Break the phrase and reorder it
Use the whole phrase as it is; do not break it or change its words
mcqs.q: How must a compound preposition be used?
mcqs.why: The rules say: use the whole phrase as it is; do not break it or change its words. Compound prepositions are learned as fixed phrases, like because of / due to / on account of for reason.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Type 3 Conditional Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

A conditional sentence has an if-clause and a main clause. Type 1 (real future): If + present simple, will + base verb — 'If we cut trees at the present speed, we will endanger our oxygen supply.' Type 2 (unreal present): If + past simple, would + base verb — 'If I were you, I would apply for the job.' Type 3 (unreal past — the subject of this lesson): If + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle — 'If you had taken your umbrella, you would have avoided getting wet in the rain.' Type 3 talks about a past situation that did not happen and imagines its different result.

Type 1 Examples (Revision)

SentencePattern
We will destroy all our wildlife if we are not careful.will + if + present
If we dump all sorts of chemicals into rivers, we will pollute them.if + present, will
If the global temperature increases, the sea levels will rise.if + present, will
The traffic flow will be better if everyone follows the traffic rules.will + if + present
You will get better marks next time if you spend less time on video games.will + if + present

Type 2 Examples (Revision)

SentencePattern
If you wore dark glasses, you would protect your eyes.if + past, would
If I won a lottery I would buy a new computer.if + past, would
I would do this work for you if time permitted.would + if + past
If the police tried hard enough they would send the thief to prison.if + past, would
It would give me a lot of pleasure if they accepted the gift.would + if + past

Type 3 Examples

SentencePattern
If the flight had arrived on time, my boss would have come to the meeting.if + had arrived, would have come
They would have eaten all the food if I had kept it on the table.would have eaten + if + had kept
If the driver had stopped at the turning, the old woman would have crossed the road easily.if + had stopped, would have crossed
I would have escaped the storm if I had been more cautious.would have escaped + if + had been
The people would have left if they had known that there was no food.would have left + if + had known
There would have been no fight if the police had arrived in time.would have been + if + had arrived
If he had attempted the question the teacher would have given him some marks.if + had attempted, would have given

Sheeba's Responses (Exercise 8)

  • 'What if you had lost?' — If I had lost, I would have cried.
  • 'How would your parents have felt?' — If I had failed, my parents would have been very disappointed.
  • 'What about your friends?' — Some would have made fun of me while a few would have encouraged me to try again.
  • 'What could you have done differently?' — I would have selected a different song if I had thought about it.
  • 'Anything else?' — My self-esteem would have been badly affected if I had performed badly.

Remember

Type 1: if + present, will. Type 2: if + past, would. Type 3: if + had + participle, would have + participle. Only Type 3 looks back at a past that cannot change now.

options: If + present simple, will + base verb
If + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle
If + past simple, would + base verb
mcqs.q: What is the structure of a Type 3 conditional sentence?
mcqs.why: Type 3 is: If + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle — 'If you had taken your umbrella, you would have avoided getting wet in the rain.' Type 1 uses present + will, and Type 2 uses past + would.

options: A past situation that did not happen, imagining its different result
mcqs.q: What does Type 3 talk about?
mcqs.why: Type 3 (unreal past) talks about a past situation that did not happen and imagines its different result. Only Type 3 looks back at a past that cannot change now.

options: If the flight had arrived on time, my boss would have come to the meeting
If we cut trees, we will endanger our oxygen supply
If I were you, I would apply for the job
If the temperature increases, sea levels will rise
mcqs.q: Which sentence is Type 3?
mcqs.why: 'If the flight had arrived on time, my boss would have come to the meeting' follows had + participle / would have + participle. The tree and temperature sentences are Type 1, and 'If I were you' is Type 2.

options: 'If I won a lottery I would buy a new computer'
'We will destroy all our wildlife if we are not careful'
'If you had taken your umbrella, you would have avoided getting wet in the rain'
'You will get better marks if you spend less time on video games'
mcqs.q: Which is the lesson's own Type 3 example about rain?
mcqs.why: The rules introduce Type 3 with: 'If you had taken your umbrella, you would have avoided getting wet in the rain.' The lottery sentence is Type 2, and the wildlife and marks sentences are Type 1.

options: would have crossed the road easily
mcqs.q: 'If the driver had stopped at the turning, the old woman ___'
mcqs.why: The Type 3 example completes: 'the old woman would have crossed the road easily.' A past perfect if-clause (had stopped) always pairs with would have + past participle in the main clause.

options: If I had lost, I will cry
If I lost, I would cry now
If I had lost, I would cry
If I had lost, I would have cried
mcqs.q: Sheeba's answer to 'What if you had lost?' is:
mcqs.why: Sheeba answers in Type 3: 'If I had lost, I would have cried.' Her other answers follow the same pattern — 'If I had failed, my parents would have been very disappointed.'

options: My self-esteem would have been badly affected if I had performed badly
My self-esteem will be affected if I perform badly
I would select a different song
Some would have made fun of me
mcqs.q: What does Sheeba say about performing badly?
mcqs.why: Her last answer is: 'My self-esteem would have been badly affected if I had performed badly.' The different-song answer belongs to 'What could you have done differently?', and the made-fun-of answer to 'What about your friends?'

options: Type 1: if + present simple, will + base verb (real future)
mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct for Type 1?
mcqs.why: The Remember section fixes the three patterns: Type 1: if + present, will. Type 2: if + past, would. Type 3: if + had + participle, would have + participle.

options: 'If the police tried hard enough they would send the thief to prison'
'If he had attempted the question the teacher would have given him some marks'
'There would have been no fight if the police had arrived in time'
'They would have eaten all the food if I had kept it on the table'
mcqs.q: Which sentence is Type 2 (unreal present)?
mcqs.why: 'If the police tried hard enough they would send the thief to prison' uses if + past simple with would — the Type 2 pattern. The other three use had + participle with would have, so they are Type 3.

options: had known, in 'The people would have left if they had known that there was no food'
mcqs.q: Which form completes the Type 3 example about the people and food?
mcqs.why: The example reads: 'The people would have left if they had known that there was no food.' The if-clause needs the past perfect, had + past participle (known).

lessons.title: Writing: Persuasive Essay
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 7.4 Writing teaches the persuasive essay — an essay that convinces the reader to agree with the writer. Persuasion uses three appeals: Emotion (feelings), Logic (facts, figures and research), and Ethics and Credibility (the writer's character and expertise).

The Three Appeals in the Exercises

StatementAppeal
Thousands of poor little children suffer a harsh, painful death every day without food or aid due to political instability.Emotion
A 45% decrease in the mortality rate has been witnessed after the vaccination drive against Corona Virus.Logic
As a doctor, I can tell you that this course of treatment will likely generate the best results.Ethics and Credibility
If we don't move soon, we're all going to die! Can't you see how dangerous it would be to stay?Emotion
I have written a lot on this topic and presented my work at a number of international conferences.Ethics and Credibility
Many people are lying under the open sky since the earthquake two weeks ago hoping that someone would help them.Emotion
This claim has been verified by research in 75 countries, over a period of seven years.Logic
The writer of this article is a world renowned pharmacist, who has been working this field for over twenty years.Ethics and Credibility

Model Essay: Girls Should Be Educated

Every girl has the right to education, yet many girls are still kept out of school. Girls should be educated because education builds a better family, a better society, and a better country. First, an educated girl becomes a better mother and a better manager of her home. She can look after the health of her children, help them in their studies, and run her home wisely. An educated mother gives her children a good start in life. Second, an educated girl can earn and support her family. She can become a teacher, a doctor, a nurse, or a businesswoman. When girls work, families become stronger and poverty decreases. Some people say that girls do not need education because they will only look after the home. This is wrong: even to look after a home well, a girl needs knowledge. An educated girl manages her home better and also guides her children. In short, girls must be educated. A nation that educates its girls educates its future. Let us send every girl to school.

The Other Essay Topics (Pattern)

  • Sports and games should be made compulsory for all students — health (fit body, strong heart and muscles, fewer illnesses), character (discipline, teamwork, fair play); answer to the objection 'sports waste study time': players are fresh and learn better.
  • Students should be encouraged to speak in English in the School — daily practice builds fluency and confidence; English is needed for interviews, jobs and higher studies; objection 'it harms our own language' answered: learning English does not mean leaving our own language.
  • Students should be guided and supported to grow some vegetables at home — teaches responsibility, patience and how nature works; fresh, healthy, cheap food; objection 'no time' answered: a small patch needs only a few minutes a day.
  • Knowledge about diseases and vaccinations should be made a part of the Curriculum — students protect themselves and their families; vaccination knowledge removes fear and false ideas; objection 'curriculum already full' answered: a few health lessons can save many lives.

Remember

Persuasive essay pattern: state your position, give reasoned points (First, Second), face the opposite view and answer it ('Some people say… This is wrong: …'), and close with 'In short…' and a call to action ('Let us…').

options: An essay that convinces the reader to agree with the writer
An essay that only explains facts
An essay that tells a personal story
An essay that describes a place
mcqs.q: What is a persuasive essay?
mcqs.why: Unit 7.4 teaches the persuasive essay — an essay that convinces the reader to agree with the writer. It works through three appeals: Emotion, Logic, and Ethics and Credibility.

options: Emotion (feelings), Logic (facts, figures and research), and Ethics and Credibility (character and expertise)
mcqs.q: What are the three appeals of persuasion?
mcqs.why: Persuasion uses three appeals: Emotion (feelings), Logic (facts, figures and research), and Ethics and Credibility (the writer's character and expertise). The exercise statements are sorted under these three heads.

mcqs.q: 'Thousands of poor little children suffer a harsh, painful death every day without food or aid' — which appeal is this?
mcqs.why: The table marks this statement Emotion: it aims at the reader's feelings about suffering children. Logic would need figures or research, and Ethics would rest on the writer's standing.

options: Logic, because it gives a figure: 'A 45% decrease in the mortality rate has been witnessed after the vaccination drive'
mcqs.q: Which appeal uses a percentage figure from a vaccination drive?
mcqs.why: The statement 'A 45% decrease in the mortality rate has been witnessed after the vaccination drive against Corona Virus' is marked Logic. Figures and verified research are the marks of the logical appeal.

options: Ethics and Credibility — 'As a doctor, I can tell you that this course of treatment will likely generate the best results'
mcqs.q: 'As a doctor, I can tell you…' is which appeal?
mcqs.why: The table marks the doctor's statement Ethics and Credibility: the writer's profession and expertise make the claim trustworthy. The pharmacist of twenty years is the same kind of appeal.

options: An educated girl becomes a better mother and a better manager of her home
mcqs.q: What is the first reason in 'Girls Should Be Educated'?
mcqs.why: First, an educated girl becomes a better mother and a better manager of her home: she can look after her children's health, help them in their studies, and run her home wisely, giving her children a good start in life.

options: They should stay at home only
An educated girl can earn and support her family — as a teacher, a doctor, a nurse, or a businesswoman
mcqs.q: What is the second reason in the model essay?
mcqs.why: Second, an educated girl can earn and support her family; she can become a teacher, a doctor, a nurse, or a businesswoman. When girls work, families become stronger and poverty decreases.

options: It is moved to the conclusion
It is faced and answered: 'Some people say that girls do not need education… This is wrong: even to look after a home well, a girl needs knowledge'
mcqs.q: How does the model essay treat the opposite view?
mcqs.why: The essay faces the objection — 'Some people say that girls do not need education because they will only look after the home' — and answers it: 'This is wrong: even to look after a home well, a girl needs knowledge.'

options: 'In short, girls must be educated… Let us send every girl to school'
mcqs.q: How does the model essay close?
mcqs.why: It closes with the pattern's ending: 'In short, girls must be educated. A nation that educates its girls educates its future. Let us send every girl to school.' — a summary plus a call to action.

options: Hide your position until the end
State your position, give reasoned points (First, Second), face the opposite view and answer it, and close with 'In short…' and a call to action
mcqs.q: What is the persuasive essay pattern?
mcqs.why: The Remember section gives the pattern: state your position, give reasoned points (First, Second), face the opposite view and answer it ('Some people say… This is wrong: …'), and close with 'In short…' and a call to action ('Let us…').

lessons.title: Study Skills: Diary Writing
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 7.5 Study Skills teaches diary writing: keep a notebook set aside for the purpose and write in it regularly, following the guidelines — write the day and date, add the time, address the diary ('Dear Diary'), record the day's main events and your feelings honestly, and close with a line about writing again.

Model Diary Entry

Saturday, 17 October 2026. 9:00 pm. Dear Diary, Today was a happy day. I went to school in the morning and my teacher praised my English essay. In the evening, I played cricket with my friends. I feel thankful for my good day. I will write my diary again tomorrow. Ahmed.

Remember

A diary is personal and regular: date and time first, then what happened, then how you felt. Writing a diary daily improves both writing skill and memory of your own learning.

options: A notebook set aside for the purpose, written in regularly
mcqs.q: What does diary writing need, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson says: keep a notebook set aside for the purpose and write in it regularly. A diary is personal and regular — a loose paper used once is not a diary habit.

options: Write the day and date, and add the time
mcqs.q: What is written first in a diary entry?
mcqs.why: The guidelines begin: write the day and date, add the time, then address the diary ('Dear Diary'). The model entry opens exactly so: 'Saturday, 17 October 2026. 9:00 pm. Dear Diary,…'

mcqs.q: How is the diary addressed?
mcqs.why: The guidelines say to address the diary as 'Dear Diary'. The model entry follows this after the date and time, which makes the diary feel like a personal companion.

options: The day's main events and your feelings, honestly
mcqs.q: What should a diary entry record?
mcqs.why: The guidelines say: record the day's main events and your feelings honestly. In the model, the events are school and cricket, and the honest feeling is thankfulness for the good day.

mcqs.q: How should a diary entry close?
mcqs.why: The guidelines end: close with a line about writing again. The model closes: 'I will write my diary again tomorrow. Ahmed.' — promise first, then the writer's name.

mcqs.q: What are the day, date and time of the model diary entry?
mcqs.why: The model entry is headed: 'Saturday, 17 October 2026. 9:00 pm.' Date and time come first in every entry, before the 'Dear Diary' address and the day's account.

options: His teacher praised his English essay
mcqs.q: What happy event does the model entry record from school?
mcqs.why: Ahmed writes: 'I went to school in the morning and my teacher praised my English essay.' In the evening he played cricket with his friends, and he closes feeling thankful for his good day.

options: He played cricket with his friends
mcqs.q: What did Ahmed do in the evening in the model entry?
mcqs.why: The model says: 'In the evening, I played cricket with my friends.' The entry keeps the day's order — school in the morning first, then the evening's game.

mcqs.q: What feeling does the model entry record?
mcqs.why: Ahmed writes: 'I feel thankful for my good day.' Feelings are recorded honestly in a diary, and here the feeling matches the day's happy events — praise at school and cricket with friends.

options: It improves both writing skill and memory of your own learning
It is only for keeping secrets
It is only for famous writers
mcqs.q: What is the benefit of writing a diary daily?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says writing a diary daily improves both writing skill and memory of your own learning. A diary is personal and regular: date and time first, then what happened, then how you felt.

lessons.title: Fun: Word Association

About the Text

Unit 7.6 Fun is a vocabulary game, Word Association: the class is divided into groups named after flowers — Rose, Jasmine, Tulip, Sunflower. The teacher calls a number and asks for words of a category; quick, correct answers win points, and the group with the most points wins.

CategoryWords
Animalscat, dog, lion, horse, goat
Birdssparrow, crow, pigeon, parrot, duck
Flowersrose, jasmine, tulip, sunflower, lily

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Safety Measures That Can Save Your Life
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The text Safety Measures That Can Save Your Life is about the importance of two safety measures: wearing helmets while riding a motorbike, and fastening seat belts while travelling in a car. We hear about fatal road accidents almost every day; recently a motorbike rider died because he was not wearing a helmet. A helmet is important safety gear because it absorbs the impact of a crash or fall and minimises head injuries — the most common cause of death and disability in motorbike accidents; brain injury can lead to permanent disability, and riders who do not wear helmets are three times more likely to suffer head injuries. A helmet also protects the eyes from wind, sun rays, dust and cold: wind, sun rays and dust particles can hinder vision leading to unexpected problems, long-term exposure can result in major eye-related health issues, and in winter a helmet makes a ride comfortable and safe. People give poor reasons for not wearing helmets: their hairstyle gets messed up, helmets feel uncomfortable, they cannot put up with the heat and sweating, or they are simply sure they will not be injured. For cars, wearing or not wearing a seat belt can be a matter of life and death. When a car stops suddenly, the car stops but the body keeps travelling at the speed of the car, and without a seat belt the body can be thrown out or go through the windshield and suffer serious injury or death. The click of a seat belt is an insurance that safeguards your safety and survival: it requires only a little effort, saves you from unnecessary expenses, high medical expenses and fines, and protects your earning capability — though it mostly keeps you safe rather than guaranteeing no harm. Every time you get into your car you make a choice between safety and harm.

Does wearing a seat belt guarantee no harm?Box E
Seat belts: summaryBox F

Reasons For and Against

Seat beltStops the body from flying through the windshield when the car stops suddenly; saves from serious injury or death; saves from high medical expenses and fines; saves the family from sufferingThey think seat belts cramp their style; they think seat belts are uncomfortable; they think seat belts are not necessary; they want ease and comfort instead of safety

Vocabulary

WordMeaning

untowardunexpected
optionchoice

Remember

Not wearing a helmet increases the chances of severe injuries, and not wearing a seat belt can lead to high medical expenses, depending on how serious the injuries are. In Exercise 8, groups role-play panel discussions and reporter interviews on helmets and seat belts; the shared conclusion is that helmets and seat belts save lives.

options: Wearing helmets while riding a motorbike, and fastening seat belts while travelling in a car
mcqs.q: Which two safety measures does the text teach?
mcqs.why: The text is about the importance of two safety measures: wearing helmets while riding a motorbike, and fastening seat belts while travelling in a car. Both measures can save your life, as the title says.

options: It absorbs the impact of a crash or fall and minimises head injuries
mcqs.q: Why is a helmet important safety gear?
mcqs.why: A helmet absorbs the impact of a crash or fall and minimises head injuries — the most common cause of death and disability in motorbike accidents. Brain injury can lead to permanent disability.

mcqs.q: Riders who do not wear helmets are how much more likely to suffer head injuries?
mcqs.why: The summary states riders who do not wear helmets are three times more likely to suffer head injuries. This figure is the text's strongest argument for wearing a helmet.

options: It protects the eyes from wind, sun rays, dust and cold
mcqs.q: What other protection does a helmet give?
mcqs.why: A helmet also protects the eyes from wind, sun rays, dust and cold: wind, sun rays and dust particles can hinder vision, long-term exposure can cause major eye problems, and in winter a helmet makes a ride comfortable and safe.

options: They are all true safety facts
Their hairstyle gets messed up, helmets feel uncomfortable, they cannot put up with the heat and sweating, or they are sure they will not be injured
Helmets are too costly for everyone
mcqs.q: What poor reasons do people give for not wearing helmets?
mcqs.why: The text calls them poor reasons: their hairstyle gets messed up, helmets feel uncomfortable, they cannot put up with the heat and sweating, or they are simply sure they will not be injured. Comfort is chosen over safety.

options: The body stops with the car
The car stops but the body keeps travelling at the speed of the car, and without a seat belt the body can be thrown out or go through the windshield
mcqs.q: What happens when a car stops suddenly without a seat belt?
mcqs.why: When a car stops suddenly, the car stops but the body keeps travelling at the speed of the car, and without a seat belt the body can be thrown out or go through the windshield and suffer serious injury or death.

options: An insurance that safeguards your safety and survival
A guarantee of no harm at all
mcqs.q: What is the click of a seat belt called in the text?
mcqs.why: The text says: the click of a seat belt is an insurance that safeguards your safety and survival. It mostly keeps you safe rather than guaranteeing no harm, as Box E discusses.

options: Both riders and pillion riders should wear helmets
mcqs.q: Who should wear a helmet, according to the reasons table?
mcqs.why: The 'for' reasons end by noting both riders and pillion riders should wear helmets. A pillion is a passenger on a motorbike, as the vocabulary list explains.

mcqs.q: What does 'fatal' mean?
mcqs.why: The vocabulary gives fatal = causing death, as in the fatal road accidents we hear about almost every day. Other words: crucial = very important, pillion = a passenger on a motorbike, safeguards = protects.

options: Helmets and seat belts are optional extras
Helmets and seat belts save lives
mcqs.q: What is the shared conclusion of the lesson?
mcqs.why: The Remember section records the shared conclusion of the panel discussions and interviews in Exercise 8: helmets and seat belts save lives. Every time you get into your car you make a choice between safety and harm.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Debate
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 8.2 Oral Communication teaches debate: speak in favour of a motion, speak against it, and finish with a rebuttal that answers the other side. A debate speech begins with the motion, gives reasons and examples, and ends with a firm conclusion: 'So … is better.'

Debate Topics and Arguments

MotionIn favourAgainstRebuttal
We have a better life than our ancestorsWe have electricity, clean water, fast transport, modern medicine, mobile phones and the internet; our ancestors suffered from diseases that are now curedAncestors lived in clean air, ate pure food, lived a simple, peaceful life with strong family bonds and no stressAlthough modern life has stress, modern facilities save lives and time; our ancestors died young from diseases we can now cure
Village life is better than city lifeVillages have clean air, fresh food, peace and quiet, and friendly neighbours; a simple and healthy lifeCities have good schools, hospitals, jobs, electricity and all facilities; villages lack themAlthough cities have facilities, they also have pollution, noise, crime and stress; health, peace and happiness are more important than facilities
Mobile phones are a source of problemsStudents waste time on games and social media and their studies suffer; phones harm eyes and health and spread false newsPhones are a source of knowledge; they help us learn, communicate and work from anywhereAlthough mobile phones have benefits, their misuse causes problems; students who use them too much fail in studies

Remember

Debate pattern: 'In favour…' — 'Against…' — 'Rebuttal: Although the other side is right that…, still…' A good rebuttal first admits the other side's strongest point, then answers it.

options: Speak in favour of a motion, speak against it, and finish with a rebuttal that answers the other side
mcqs.q: What three parts does a debate have in this lesson?
mcqs.why: Unit 8.2 teaches debate: speak in favour of a motion, speak against it, and finish with a rebuttal that answers the other side. The pattern is 'In favour…' — 'Against…' — 'Rebuttal'.

options: 'So … is better' — a debate speech ends with a firm conclusion
mcqs.q: How does a debate speech end?
mcqs.why: A debate speech begins with the motion, gives reasons and examples, and ends with a firm conclusion: 'So … is better.' The conclusion states the side's final judgment plainly.

options: It repeats your own first point
It first admits the other side's strongest point, then answers it: 'Although the other side is right that…, still…'
mcqs.q: What makes a good rebuttal?
mcqs.why: The Remember section says a good rebuttal first admits the other side's strongest point, then answers it. The debate table's rebuttals all begin with 'Although…' before giving the answer.

options: No stress and strong family bonds
Electricity, clean water, fast transport, modern medicine, mobile phones and the internet
mcqs.q: For 'We have a better life than our ancestors', what is argued in favour?
mcqs.why: In favour: we have electricity, clean water, fast transport, modern medicine, mobile phones and the internet; our ancestors suffered from diseases that are now cured. The clean air and family bonds points belong to the against side.

options: Modern facilities save lives and time; our ancestors died young from diseases we can now cure
mcqs.q: What is the rebuttal for the ancestors motion?
mcqs.why: The rebuttal admits modern life has stress, but answers: modern facilities save lives and time; our ancestors died young from diseases we can now cure. It concedes a point, then outweighs it.

options: Villages have clean air, fresh food, peace and quiet, and friendly neighbours — a simple and healthy life
mcqs.q: For 'Village life is better than city life', what is argued in favour?
mcqs.why: In favour of village life: villages have clean air, fresh food, peace and quiet, and friendly neighbours; a simple and healthy life. The against side answers that cities have good schools, hospitals, jobs and electricity.

options: Although cities have facilities, they also have pollution, noise, crime and stress; health, peace and happiness are more important than facilities
mcqs.q: What is the rebuttal in the village-versus-city debate?
mcqs.why: The rebuttal admits cities have facilities, but answers that they also have pollution, noise, crime and stress — and health, peace and happiness are more important than facilities. This is the admit-then-answer pattern.

options: Phones are a source of knowledge
Phones help us work from anywhere
Students waste time on games and social media and their studies suffer; phones harm eyes and health and spread false news
mcqs.q: Which points support the motion 'Mobile phones are a source of problems'?
mcqs.why: In favour of the motion: students waste time on games and social media and their studies suffer; phones harm eyes and health and spread false news. The knowledge and communication points are the against side's case.

options: Although mobile phones have benefits, their misuse causes problems; students who use them too much fail in studies
Phones have no benefits at all
All students fail because of phones
Phones should be banned by law
mcqs.q: What is the rebuttal in the mobile-phones debate?
mcqs.why: The rebuttal admits the other side's point — although mobile phones have benefits, their misuse causes problems; students who use them too much fail in studies. Admitting a benefit first makes the answer stronger.

options: Reasons and examples support each side, after the speech begins with the motion
mcqs.q: What does a debate speech contain after the motion?
mcqs.why: The lesson says a debate speech begins with the motion, gives reasons and examples, and ends with a firm conclusion. Each motion in the table is supported by listed reasons on both sides.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Revision of Relative Pronouns
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Relative pronouns join a describing clause to a noun: who for people as subject (Albert Einstein was a scientist who made many important discoveries); whom for people as object (This is the person whom we met last week); whose for possession (We met our friend whose father passed away last month); which for things (Pizza is a popular food which was first made in Italy); that for people or things (A helicopter is a machine that can fly; This is the house that Jamil built). When the relative clause adds extra information about a named person or thing, it is set off with commas: 'Shahid, who gave a long and tedious speech, won the prize.'

Examples

SentencePoint shown
The festival which lasted all day, ended with a banquet.which — thing, subject
I am looking for someone who can watch my dog while I go on vacation.who — person, subject
The police needed details that could help identify the robber.that — thing, subject
I'd like to take you to a café which serves excellent coffee.which — thing, subject
I cannot say goodbye to one whose personality I have always liked.whose — possession
I saw the shoes that you bought last week on sale for less this week.that — thing, object
This is the person whom we met last week.whom — person, object
I have a watch which is ten years old.which — thing, subject
Mr Liaquat whose house is next to our house is an engineer.whose — possession
I bought a cell phone which has 5G internet access.which — thing, subject
Mosquitoes are insects that like to bite people.that — things, subject
My uncle whom we met last night helps us with our homework.whom — person, object
Shah Inayat Shaheed is a famous Sufi saint who has millions of followers.who — person, subject
A blanket is something that people use in winter.that — thing, object

Combining Sentences

Two sentencesCombined
Shahid gave a long and tedious speech. He won the prize.Shahid, who gave a long and tedious speech, won the prize.
A chain of stores wants to open new stores across the province. It does business all over Pakistan.A chain of stores, which does business all over Pakistan, wants to open new stores across the province.
Scientists are working on stem cells. Stem cells will revolutionize medicine.Scientists are working on stem cells, which will revolutionize medicine.
Last week, Rizwan interviewed Sana. She is my neighbour.Last week, Rizwan interviewed Sana, who is my neighbour.
Yesterday I met a talented man. He works in a circus.Yesterday I met a talented man who works in a circus.
John F. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963. He was the president of the USA.John F. Kennedy, who was the president of the USA, was assassinated in 1963.
The prime minister will inaugurate a new hospital. It is on 6th street.The prime minister will inaugurate a new hospital, which is on 6th street.
He sat on the wooden chair. The chair was broken.He sat on the wooden chair, which was broken.

Remember

Choose by the noun and its job in the clause: person + subject = who; person + object = whom; possession = whose; thing = which/that. 'What' is not used as a relative pronoun in these exercises.

mcqs.q: Which relative pronoun is used for people as subject?
mcqs.why: Who is used for people as subject: 'Albert Einstein was a scientist who made many important discoveries.' Whom is for people as object, whose for possession, and which for things.

options: whom, in 'This is the person whom we met last week'
mcqs.q: Which pronoun is used for people as object?
mcqs.why: Whom is used for people as object: 'This is the person whom we met last week.' The Remember rule sorts by the noun and its job: person + subject = who; person + object = whom.

options: whose, in 'We met our friend whose father passed away last month'
mcqs.q: Which pronoun shows possession?
mcqs.why: Whose shows possession: 'We met our friend whose father passed away last month.' Another example is 'Mr Liaquat whose house is next to our house is an engineer.'

options: which, in 'Pizza is a popular food which was first made in Italy'
mcqs.q: Which pronoun is used for things in the pizza example?
mcqs.why: Which is used for things: 'Pizza is a popular food which was first made in Italy.' That can also be used for people or things, as in 'the house that Jamil built'.

options: For people or things: 'A helicopter is a machine that can fly; This is the house that Jamil built'
mcqs.q: What can 'that' refer to?
mcqs.why: That is used for people or things: 'A helicopter is a machine that can fly' (thing) and the lesson also gives 'that' for people in its rule line. Which, by contrast, is for things.

options: When the relative clause adds extra information about a named person or thing, it is set off with commas
mcqs.q: When is a relative clause set off with commas?
mcqs.why: The rules say: when the relative clause adds extra information about a named person or thing, it is set off with commas — 'Shahid, who gave a long and tedious speech, won the prize.' Shahid is already named, so the clause is extra.

options: 'Shahid, who gave a long and tedious speech, won the prize'
'Shahid who gave a long speech won prize'
'Shahid, which gave a speech, won the prize'
'Shahid whom gave a speech won the prize'
mcqs.q: How are 'Shahid gave a long and tedious speech. He won the prize.' combined?
mcqs.why: The combining table gives: 'Shahid, who gave a long and tedious speech, won the prize.' Who is right for a person as subject, and commas set off the extra information about the named Shahid.

options: 'Scientists are working on stem cells what will revolutionize medicine'
'Scientists are working on stem cells who will revolutionize medicine'
'Scientists are working on stem cells, which will revolutionize medicine'
'Scientists are working on stem cells whom will revolutionize medicine'
mcqs.q: How are the stem-cell sentences combined?
mcqs.why: The combined sentence is: 'Scientists are working on stem cells, which will revolutionize medicine.' Which is used for things, and 'what' is not used as a relative pronoun in these exercises.

options: 'Yesterday I met a talented man which works in a circus'
'Yesterday I met a talented man who works in a circus'
'Yesterday I met a talented man whom works in a circus'
'Yesterday I met a talented man whose works in a circus'
mcqs.q: How are 'Yesterday I met a talented man. He works in a circus.' combined?
mcqs.why: The combined sentence is: 'Yesterday I met a talented man who works in a circus.' The man is a person and the subject of 'works', so who is used, with no commas because the clause identifies which man.

options: Choose by the noun and its job in the clause: person + subject = who; person + object = whom; possession = whose; thing = which/that
mcqs.q: What is the rule for choosing a relative pronoun?
mcqs.why: The Remember section gives the selection rule: person + subject = who; person + object = whom; possession = whose; thing = which/that. 'What' is not used as a relative pronoun in these exercises.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Direct and Indirect Speech — Commands and Requests
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Commands and requests in indirect speech are reported with a reporting verb + object + to-infinitive. Choose the reporting verb by tone: ordered for authority (teacher, guard, officer, commander, principal, boss), requested for polite requests with 'please', asked for neutral requests, advised for advice, told for plain instructions. Negative commands use not to: 'Do not talk during the assembly' → The teacher ordered the students not to talk during the assembly. Change pronouns and words like this → that where needed, and the tense inside any following clause (are → were).

Orders Reported

DirectIndirect
The teacher said to the students, 'Do not talk during the assembly.'The teacher ordered the students not to talk during the assembly.
Mother said to her son, 'Work hard or else you will fail.'Mother told her son to work hard or else he would fail.
The guard said to us, 'Stand in the queue and wait for your turn.'The guard ordered us to stand in the queue and wait for our turn.
The officer said to the peon, 'Let the visitor come in.'The officer ordered the peon to let the visitor come in.
'Stay indoors during the storm,' the government authorities advised the people.The government authorities advised the people to stay indoors during the storm.
'Go away and never come back again,' said his boss.His boss ordered him to go away and never come back again.
The principal said to the naughty student, 'Come after school hours.'The principal ordered the naughty student to come after school hours.
'Soldiers, march quickly to the exit,' said the commander.The commander ordered the soldiers to march quickly to the exit.
The clerk said to the man, 'Do not disturb me.'The clerk told the man not to disturb him.

Requests Reported

DirectIndirect
'Try to speak gently when talking to old people,' the manager said to his staff.The manager requested his staff to try to speak gently when talking to old people.
'Please turn out the lights, team, when you leave the room,' said the organizer.The organizer requested the team to turn out the lights when they left the room.
'Give me a glass of water, Yusuf,' said grandfather.Grandfather asked Yusuf to give him a glass of water.
'Sana, please put this plate on the table,' said Mrs Sultan.Mrs Sultan requested Sana to put that plate on the table.
'Make sure that the children are in bed by eight o'clock,' said father.Father asked them to make sure that the children were in bed by eight o'clock.
The doctor said to the patient, 'Take your medicines on time.'The doctor advised the patient to take his medicines on time.
'Please be seated,' said the announcer.The announcer requested them to be seated.
'Never say no when someone asks for help,' the preacher said in his speech.The preacher advised in his speech never to say no when someone asks for help.
'Be quiet, please, children,' said the mother.The mother requested the children to be quiet.
'Water the plants before you go,' said my father to the gardener.My father asked the gardener to water the plants before he went.

Remember

Pattern: reporting verb + person + (not) to + base verb. Exercise 7 reports a whole classroom dialogue the same way: 'The teacher told the class to hurry up as they were getting late… The teacher ordered them to get out of the classroom before the guests came… The teacher told them to wait outside until all the guests were seated.'

mcqs.q: How are commands and requests reported in indirect speech?
mcqs.why: Commands and requests are reported with a reporting verb + object + to-infinitive: 'The guard ordered us to stand in the queue.' The verb is chosen by tone, and negative commands use 'not to'.

options: ordered, for authority — teacher, guard, officer, commander, principal, boss
mcqs.q: Which reporting verb is used for authority?
mcqs.why: The rules match verbs to tone: ordered for authority (teacher, guard, officer, commander, principal, boss), requested for polite requests with 'please', asked for neutral requests, advised for advice, and told for plain instructions.

options: not to talk, in 'The teacher ordered the students not to talk during the assembly'
mcqs.q: How is 'Do not talk during the assembly' reported?
mcqs.why: Negative commands use not to: 'The teacher ordered the students not to talk during the assembly.' The same form reports the clerk's words: 'The clerk told the man not to disturb him.'

options: The principal requested the student to come
The principal asked the student to come politely
The principal suggested the student to come
The principal ordered the naughty student to come after school hours
mcqs.q: 'Come after school hours,' the principal said to the naughty student. Reported:
mcqs.why: The table gives: 'The principal ordered the naughty student to come after school hours.' A principal speaking to a naughty student is authority, so 'ordered' is the right verb.

options: The officer ordered the peon to let the visitor come in
The officer asked the peon if the visitor came in
The officer requested the peon to let the visitor come in please
The officer said the peon to let the visitor come in
mcqs.q: 'Let the visitor come in,' the officer said to the peon. Reported:
mcqs.why: The reported form is: 'The officer ordered the peon to let the visitor come in.' An officer's instruction to a peon carries authority, and the pattern is verb + object + to-infinitive.

options: advised, in 'The doctor advised the patient to take his medicines on time'
mcqs.q: 'Take your medicines on time,' the doctor said to the patient. Which verb fits?
mcqs.why: The doctor's words are advice, so the table reports: 'The doctor advised the patient to take his medicines on time.' Advised is the verb for advice, as with the government authorities advising people to stay indoors during the storm.

options: Grandfather ordered Yusuf to give him a glass of water
Grandfather asked Yusuf to give him a glass of water
Grandfather requested Yusuf that he gives water
Grandfather told Yusuf give him water
mcqs.q: 'Give me a glass of water, Yusuf,' said grandfather. Reported:
mcqs.why: The table gives: 'Grandfather asked Yusuf to give him a glass of water.' It is a neutral family request, so 'asked' is used, and 'me' becomes 'him' in the reported form.

options: requested Sana to put this plate here
ordered Sana to put the plate loudly
requested Sana to put that plate on the table — 'this' changes to 'that'
mcqs.q: 'Sana, please put this plate on the table,' said Mrs Sultan. Reported correctly:
mcqs.why: With 'please', the verb is requested: 'Mrs Sultan requested Sana to put that plate on the table.' The rules also require changing words like this → that where needed.

options: requested his staff to try to speak gently when talking to old people
asked his staff if they speak gently
told his staff that speak gently
mcqs.q: 'Try to speak gently when talking to old people,' the manager said to his staff. Reported:
mcqs.why: The table reports: 'The manager requested his staff to try to speak gently when talking to old people.' The manager's polite instruction to staff takes 'requested' plus the to-infinitive.

options: Reporting verb + person + (not) to + base verb
mcqs.q: What is the pattern in the Remember section?
mcqs.why: The pattern is: reporting verb + person + (not) to + base verb. Exercise 7 applies it to a whole classroom dialogue: 'The teacher told the class to hurry up… ordered them to get out of the classroom… told them to wait outside.'

lessons.title: Writing: Argumentative Essay
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 8.4 Writing teaches the argumentative essay. Like the persuasive essay, it takes a position, but it is built on argument: an introduction with the writer's stand, body paragraphs of arguments (First, Second), a paragraph that presents the opposite view fairly ('Some people argue… It may be argued/claimed that… However…') and answers it, and a conclusion beginning 'In short'. The essay titles themselves contain conditional patterns to notice: 'If students are not promoted, they will fail; if they are promoted, they will keep learning' and 'If teachers do not punish, students will become careless'.

Model Essay: Wearing Uniforms Should Not Be Compulsory in Schools

School uniforms are a common sight, but should they be forced on every student? Wearing uniforms should not be compulsory in schools because it limits freedom, burdens poor families, and does not improve learning. First, uniforms limit students' freedom of choice. Students are individuals, and their dress is a part of their personality. Forcing all students to wear the same dress kills their individuality. Second, uniforms are a burden on poor families. Uniforms are costly, and children grow fast, so parents must buy new uniforms again and again. This is a heavy expense for poor families. Some people argue that uniforms bring equality and discipline. It may be argued that uniforms remove differences between rich and poor. However, true equality comes from respect and good behaviour, not from the same dress. Uniforms do not make students disciplined or better learners. In short, uniforms should not be compulsory. Schools should allow students to wear clean, decent clothes of their own choice. This will save money and respect students' freedom.

Model Essay: All the Students Should Be Promoted to the Next Class Without Exams

Exams cause fear and stress in students. All students should be promoted to the next class without exams because exams do not measure true ability, and they harm students' health and confidence. First, exams do not measure true ability. A student may know the subject well but fail in the exam due to fear or illness. Exams test memory, not understanding. Second, exams harm students' health and confidence. Many students suffer from stress, sleepless nights, and fear of failure. A failed student loses confidence and may leave studies. Some people argue that exams are necessary to check learning. It may be claimed that without exams students will not study. However, teachers can check learning through class work, projects, and assignments. Learning can be judged without the fear of exams. In short, all students should be promoted without exams. If students are not promoted, they will fail; if they are promoted, they will keep learning with confidence. Promotion without exams will make learning joyful.

Model Essay: Teachers Should Punish Students Who Do Not Do Their Work Properly

Some students do not do their work properly. Teachers should punish students who do not do their work properly because punishment teaches discipline, and it protects the rights of serious students. First, punishment teaches discipline. When a student is punished for not doing his work, he learns that work must be done on time. Discipline is necessary for success in life. Second, punishment protects serious students. If lazy students are not punished, serious students also become careless. Punishment keeps the whole class serious about studies. Some people argue that punishment harms students. It may be claimed that punishment makes students hate studies. However, fair and light punishment does not harm; it guides. Punishment should be fair, not cruel. In short, teachers should punish students who do not do their work properly. Fair punishment builds discipline and respect for work. If teachers do not punish, students will become careless and fail in life.

The Other Essay Topics (Pattern)

  • Students should not be allowed to bring mobile phones to school — phones disturb studies (games, videos, chat in class; attention and marks fall) and cause discipline problems (cheating, fights over expensive models); objection 'needed for safety' answered: parents can contact the school office in an emergency.
  • Gardening should be made a compulsory subject in all schools — teaches useful skills (growing vegetables, fruits and flowers; patience, responsibility, hard work), improves health and the environment; objection 'wastes study time' answered: gardening is also learning — science, nature and life — and refreshes the mind. A second model essay argues differently: gardening connects students with nature (seeds, soil, water, sun, seasons) and saves money (school garden vegetables; pots and boxes where there is no land).

Remember

Argumentative essay pattern: question or problem → your stand with reasons → First argument → Second argument → opposite view ('Some people argue… It may be claimed…') → your answer ('However…') → 'In short' conclusion. In Exercise 2, write individually on one of the topics, but not the one you have already written in the group task.

options: It takes a position, but it is built on argument: it presents the opposite view fairly and answers it
mcqs.q: How is an argumentative essay different from a persuasive essay?
mcqs.why: Like the persuasive essay, it takes a position, but it is built on argument: an introduction with the writer's stand, body paragraphs of arguments, a paragraph that presents the opposite view fairly ('Some people argue… However…') and answers it, and a conclusion beginning 'In short'.

options: Wearing uniforms should not be compulsory in schools
mcqs.q: What is the stand of the model essay on uniforms?
mcqs.why: The model's stand is that wearing uniforms should not be compulsory in schools because it limits freedom, burdens poor families, and does not improve learning. The whole essay argues this one position.

options: Uniforms limit students' freedom of choice; forcing the same dress kills individuality, since dress is part of personality
mcqs.q: What is the first argument against compulsory uniforms?
mcqs.why: First, uniforms limit students' freedom of choice: students are individuals, and their dress is a part of their personality, so forcing all students to wear the same dress kills their individuality.

options: Uniforms are costly, and children grow fast, so parents must buy new uniforms again and again — a heavy expense for poor families
mcqs.q: What is the second argument in the uniforms essay?
mcqs.why: Second, uniforms are a burden on poor families: uniforms are costly, and children grow fast, so parents must buy new uniforms again and again. This is a heavy expense for poor families.

options: Uniforms bring equality and discipline — answered: true equality comes from respect and good behaviour, not from the same dress
Rich and poor should wear different dresses
mcqs.q: What opposite view is answered in the uniforms essay?
mcqs.why: Some people argue uniforms bring equality and discipline; it may be argued they remove differences between rich and poor. However, the essay answers, true equality comes from respect and good behaviour, not from the same dress.

options: Exams do not measure true ability: a student may know the subject well but fail due to fear or illness; exams test memory, not understanding
mcqs.q: What is the first argument for promotion without exams?
mcqs.why: First, exams do not measure true ability: a student may know the subject well but fail in the exam due to fear or illness. Exams test memory, not understanding — so promotion should not depend on them.

options: Students will not study at all
Teachers can check learning through class work, projects, and assignments, without the fear of exams
mcqs.q: How is the objection 'without exams students will not study' answered?

lessons.title: Study Skills: How to Study Effectively
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 8.5 Study Skills teaches how to study effectively. The lesson is built on the principle of peak and has three areas: (1) How much to study and when to stop; (2) What to do after stopping studies upon reaching the peak; (3) How to do revision in an effective manner. First, students name their own study problems — the five most common are: forgetting what was studied after a few days; studying long hours but learning very little; feeling tired and unable to concentrate; not revising lessons regularly; and using the mobile phone while studying.

Area 1: How Much to Study and When to Stop

  • The idea 'the more time you spend in studying the more you learn' is wrong.
  • When studying, you learn quite fast until you reach your peak. After that, the forgetting starts.
  • The average peak is 5 hours; yours could be a little less or more.
  • The peak differs with every individual, with the type of work, even in the same person from week to week.
  • It is important to bear the principle of peak in mind.
  • You know you have reached your peak when you begin to feel fatigued, and you find yourself reading the same stuff without taking anything in. Stop.
  • Fatigue is natural; by pushing yourself you can only get exhausted.
  • When you study 20 hours or more, you will remember very little — probably as much as you would learn in an hour or two.

Area 2: What to Do after Stopping Studies upon Reaching the Peak

  • After studying up to the maximum point, you must not sit idle and worry but do something different.
  • Do not sit around and rest after finishing studying, because the mind does not work like the body.
  • For the mind, rest comes from doing something different. The mind gets its relaxation from variety.
  • For renewing physical energy, the body needs to rest.
  • The mind keeps working even when you are asleep. Something that was evading you will suddenly become clear when you wake up.
  • 'Let's sleep over it' is a famous saying, because the mind will work and find the answer while your body is resting.

Area 3: How to Do Revision in an Effective Manner

  • Revision is about ensuring that what you have learnt is accessible.
  • Revision is about tidying up loose ends, putting the stuff you know in order.
  • Only go over stuff you know and organise it in your mind.
  • While revising, do not learn new material. It will only lie in the way and interfere with the material you know well.

Remember

Study to your peak, then stop; rest the mind by variety, not by idleness; revise only what you know, in order, without adding new material. (Model choice in Exercise 4: the statement about the mind's rest coming from variety is the favourite, because it teaches us to play, walk or do something different after studying instead of sitting idle.)

lessons.title: Fun: Poem — The Blind Men and the Elephant
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 8.6 Fun is the poem The Blind Men and the Elephant by J. G. Saxe, to be read and acted out in groups of four. In the poem, six blind men of Indostan go to observe an elephant. Each man touches a different part and describes the whole elephant from that one part only; then they argue loudly, each sure his own view is right.

What Each Blind Man Said

Blind manPart touchedWhat he called the elephant
FirstThe sideA wall
SecondThe tuskA spear
ThirdThe trunkA snake
FourthThe kneeA tree
FifthThe earA fan
SixthThe tailA rope

Remember

The lesson of the poem: each man was partly right, but all were wrong, because they judged the whole from one part only. In the group activity, each student recites and acts out one or two verses, showing how each man touches and describes his part, and the group ends with the argument and the lesson.

mcqs.q: Who wrote the poem 'The Blind Men and the Elephant'?
mcqs.why: Unit 8.6 Fun is the poem The Blind Men and the Elephant by J. G. Saxe, to be read and acted out in groups of four. Six blind men of Indostan go to observe an elephant in the poem.

mcqs.q: How many blind men go to observe the elephant?
mcqs.why: In the poem, six blind men of Indostan go to observe an elephant. Each man touches a different part and describes the whole elephant from that one part only.

options: A wall — he touched the side
mcqs.q: The first blind man touched the side. What did he call the elephant?
mcqs.why: The table gives: First man, the side, a wall. Each man's answer matches the feel of the single part he touched — the broad, flat side felt like a wall to him.

options: A spear — he touched the tusk
mcqs.q: The second man touched the tusk. What did he call the elephant?
mcqs.why: The second man touched the tusk and called the elephant a spear — the hard, pointed tusk felt like a spear. The trunk, by contrast, felt like a snake to the third man.

options: A snake — he touched the trunk
mcqs.q: The third man touched the trunk. What did he call the elephant?
mcqs.why: The third man touched the trunk and called the elephant a snake, because the long, moving trunk felt like one. Each description is true of one part but wrong for the whole animal.

options: The knee — a tree; the ear — a fan
mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct for the fourth and fifth men?
mcqs.why: The table gives: Fourth man, the knee, a tree; Fifth man, the ear, a fan. The sixth man touched the tail and called the elephant a rope.

mcqs.q: What did the sixth man call the elephant?
mcqs.why: The sixth man touched the tail and called the elephant a rope — the thin, swinging tail felt like a rope in his hands. With this, all six part-descriptions are complete.

mcqs.why: After describing, they argued loudly, each sure his own view is right. The group activity ends with this argument and then the lesson of the poem.
